article_text:
French-Senegalese filmmaker Alain Gomis ’ “ Dao ,” an expansive family saga spanning Europe and Africa, was awarded the Golden Spike for best film at Spain’s 71st Valladolid International Film Festival ( Seminci ) while Marine Atlan’s acclaimed debut “ La Gradiva ” received the Silver Spike.

Unfolding between a wedding in France and an ancestral memorial ceremony in Guinea-Bissau, Gomis’ three-hour film blurs fiction and documentary, gathering a sprawling cast of professional and non-professional performers to explore family ties, migration and the pull of inherited traditions. The international jury praised the film’s distinctive cinematic form, citing its use of rhythm, duration and movement to create an intimate yet immersive atmosphere.

“Dao,” which world premiered in competition at Berlin, marks Gomis’ return to fiction features after “Félicité,” winner of the 2017 Berlinale Grand Jury Prize. Reviewing the new film, Variety ’s Guy Lodge called it the director’s “most vibrantly expansive and accessible” work. The Party Film Sales handles international sales while Janus Films holds North American distribution rights.

Atlan’s “La Gradiva” premiered at Cannes’ Critics’ Week, where it won its top Grand Prix, before receiving the Melbourne International Film Festival’s Bright Horizons Award in August. At Valladolid, the French-Italian feature also picked up the José Salcedo editing prize for Guillaume Lillo and the Rainbow Spike, recognizing LGBTQ-related cinema.

Set during a French school trip to Naples and Pompeii, the film follows a group of teenagers navigating desire, insecurity and the last moments of adolescence. “Seismically sensitive and deeply moving,” wrote Variety critic Jessica Kiang, who called it “one of the most piercingly accurate and immersive portrayals ever” of that precarious age. MK2 Films represents international sales.

Argentine filmmaker Lisandro Alonso, whose credits include “Jauja” and “Eureka,” earned the Ribera del Duero best director award for “Double Freedom,” the well-received sequel to his 2001 debut “Freedom,” sold by Luxbox.

Acting honors went to Alba Rohrwacher for Stéphane Brizé’s “A Good Little Soldier,” in which she plays a corporate executive caught in a system of profit at any cost, and Swann Arlaud for Emmanuel Marre’s “A Man of His Time,” about a French engineer drawn into the Vichy regime.

Marre’s film also picked up the cinematography award for Olivier Boonjing. Austrian filmmaker Sandra Wollner won the Miguel Delibes screenplay prize for “Everytime,” a drama exploring grief and memory through digital technology. The official competition jury gave a special mention to Tiago Guedes’ “Aquí.”

Beyond the main competition, Thai filmmaker Sompot Chidgasornpongse took the Meeting Point prize for “9 Temples to Heaven,” which premiered in Cannes’ Directors’ Fortnight. The contemplative family pilgrimage drama marks the fiction-feature debut of a longtime collaborator of Apichatpong Weerasethakul. Marc Ferrer’s “Cinemanía” received the Fundos Award, while Manon Coubia won the ESCAC directing prize for “Forest High.”

Spanish debut “Salen las lobas” emerged as a double audience favorite, taking both the Meeting Point Audience Award and the Seminci Youth Prize. Directed by Claudia Estrada Tarascó, the film follows girls in a juvenile justice facility who bond over music and dreams of a Barcelona trap competition. Produced by Alba Sotorra’s Oceanika, it is sold internationally by MoreThan Films and is set for a Dec. 11 Spanish theatrical release through Silencio Cinema.

In the Alchemies section, Ivan Marković’s “Promised Spaces,” a portrait of Cambodia’s rapidly transformed urban landscape, collected the Grand Prize. David Baute’s “Benigno,” about an elderly man preserving a disappearing way of life in the Canary Islands, received a special mention and the environmental Green Spike.

Hassen Ferhani’s Algeria-France production “Alea Jacarandas” took the Time of History Grand Prize, with the special award going to Mariano Llinás’ “Life of Jorge Luis Borges.” Isabelle Stever’s “I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming” received the FIPRESCI critics’ prize, while Markus Schleinzer’s “Rose” won the main competition Audience Award.

Seminci unveiled its winners Saturday morning in Valladolid after organizers canceled the traditional closing gala following a deadly train accident in Toledo province. Held Oct. 23-31, the festival’s 71st edition was led by interim co-directors Mariona Viader and Javier H. Estrada following the death of José Luis Cienfuegos last December.

Organizers reported a provisional audience tally of 100,000, more than 120 film discussions and participation by over 90% of the directors represented in its official sections. The festival closed with the Spanish premiere of Gael García Bernal’s “Hombre al agua.”

Sandra Wollner, “Everytime”

José Salcedo Award for Best Editing

Guillaume Lillo, “La Gradiva”

Special Mention

Tiago Guedes, “Aquí”

MEETING POINT

Meeting Point Award

Sompot Chidgasornpongse, “9 Temples to Heaven”

Fundos Award

Marc Ferrer, “Cinemanía”

ESCAC Award for Best Director

Manon Coubia, “Forest High”

ALCHEMIES

Grand Prize

Ivan Marković, “Promised Spaces”

Special Mention

TIME OF HISTORY

Grand Prize

Hassen Ferhani, “Alea Jacarandas”

Special Award

Mariano Llinás, “Life of Jorge Luis Borges”

DOC. Spain Award

OTHER FEATURE AWARDS

Sebastián Uría, “Adiós, ríos”

article_text:
As Taika Waititi ‘s latest directorial effort gets its time in the sun, he has some choice words for critics attempting to rain on his parade.

On Saturday, the Oscar winner boasted about Klara and the Sun ‘s 78% Rotten Tomatoes audience score (now at 73%), while slamming the “sad lost souls” who gave the movie a negative review, contributing to its 26% critics rating.

Related Stories

How ‘Klara and the Sun’ Got Blotted Out at the Box Office

Tim Burton And ‘Klara And The Sun’ Author Kazuo Ishiguro Team On Secret Project – The Dish

“I haven’t read a review of anything aimed at me or my peers in almost 15 years. But I do listen to the people,” he prefaced on Instagram .

“So this Halloween, let’s spare a thought for those sad lost souls who couldn’t achieve their dreams of becoming artists, and thus became critics. The same people who also hated Jojo Rabbit ,” added Waititi. “Irrelevant. Out of touch. Obsolete. In the bin.”

Watch on Deadline

In Deadline’s review , Damon White wrote of the Sony Pictures adaptation, “Taiki Waititi should be a snug-as-a-bug fit for Kazuo Ishiguro’s dystopian — or is it? — 2021 novel, given the director’s affinity for a very particular and peculiar kind of reality-based cringe comedy. But Klara just doesn’t deliver on any of the fronts it promises.”

Meanwhile, Waititi might have flown too close to the sun with the film’s reported $20M budget, opening last weekend to $701K domestic . Following the negative reviews out of BFI this month, Sony cut the film’s wide release to 880 theaters in the US.

Based on Kazuo Ishiguro’s 2021 dystopian novel, Klara and the Sun stars Jenna Ortega as the titular android, who is purchased as an “Artificial Friend” for gravely ill teenager Josie (Mia Tharia), whose family is mourning the death of her older sister Sal.

article_text:
W hen the call came early one morning, Tehran resident Elham Issari knew it must be urgent. The voice on the line was offering something precious. “Miss Elham,” he said excitedly, “I have a single tube of white paint! It’s overpriced and I know it’s overpriced but, if you want it, you have to buy it right now because there’s this other guy in this other city who wants it and you have to tell me within the next five minutes.”

The tube of white paint would have cost Issari 5m tomans (about $36), she recalls. “I was like, I don’t think so, because that’s overpriced, and the next thing you know is it’s 4am and I’m on YouTube watching how to make lead white in your backyard without getting lead poisoning.”

It is a revealing slice of life in Iran these days. Since the US and Israel launched joint airstrikes and combat operations on 28 February, and turned the screws on Iran’s economy, thousands of visual artists have been plunged into economic and professional limbo.

The sudden onset of war shuttered commercial galleries in central Tehran, cancelled scheduled solo exhibitions, severed shipping channels and destroyed the fragile domestic market that allows creators to pay rent and sustain studio practices.

But it was out of this systemic breakdown that Continuum: Artist Relief for Iran was born. The initiative connects contemporary artists living and working inside Iran with international audiences, collectors and institutions through a dedicated platform at iranartistrelief.org .

The project owes its existence to Dario Duran , a Canadian-Iranian curator and founder of Duran Art Projects. Born in Shiraz, but raised in Canada, Duran holds degrees in photography, art history and curatorial studies. Six years ago, driven by nostalgia and a desire to connect with his heritage, he moved to Iran, where he fell in love with the dynamism of the domestic art scene.

When war broke out, Duran found himself caught directly in its crosshairs. “I was displaced,” the 38-year-old explains from Shiraz in Iran . “My mom and dad were visiting from Canada and we had to flee Shiraz because Shiraz was being hit pretty hard every day. It was becoming unbearable. We went by ground to the north of the country, where it was relatively quiet.”

In the north, Duran encountered dozens of other displaced cultural workers who had fled bombed urban centers such as Tehran and Isfahan. He linked up there with Mariam Rasti , co-founder of Duran Art Projects, who had also fled the capital.

“We were in constant communication with the artists,” Duran recalls. “One thing we saw over and over again was that, like never before, the artists were losing hope. Cancelled exhibitions, galleries closing, not being able to find materials, artists being displaced – every single person was going through the exact same uncertainty of what happens tomorrow.”

I ran’s contemporary art world operates inside a structural bubble, isolated from international banking networks. Typically, an artist works for one or two years to prepare a body of work, relying on a single gallery showcase to generate enough sales to survive for the next two years. When conflict brought that domestic cycle to a dead halt, creators faced immediate ruin.

Duran says: “We realised that at this moment, exhibition making, curation, archiving – these things do not matter. What matters, more than anything else, is simply sales. These artists were not able to pay their rent.

“One artist put up his paintbrushes and paint tubes for sale on Divar [a classifieds site] just to carry on. Another artist told me: ‘I’m going to go work in a coffee shop for the time being because I have no idea if this art thing is going to work out for me’.”

Determined to make a difference, Duran bought a couple of gigabytes of internet access so he could get on WhatsApp. From his laptop in the north, he drafted an open letter to international collectors, museum directors and gallerists across the diaspora, laying bare the plight of creators inside Iran.

The response was immediate and overwhelming. Gallerists and curators in London, New York, Paris, Dubai, Toronto and Mumbai wrote back, eager to assist. What had originally been planned as a modest PDF catalogue featuring a dozen imperilled acquaintances rapidly transformed into a nationwide initiative.

Over five months of feverish development, Duran, Rasti and a coalition of domestic galleries built Continuum. The digital platform brings together more than 500 original artworks by over 200 contemporary artists living and working inside Iran.

Eleven commercial galleries across Iran agreed to voluntarily waive 100% of their sales commissions. Duran Art Projects charges no platform fees. As a result, 100% of every completed artwork sale goes directly to the artist. To make acquisitions realistic for global buyers during an economic downturn, prices were capped across three accessible tiers: up to $500; $500–$2,500; $2,500–$5,000.

While the online front end of Continuum offers a catalogue of striking abstract canvases, delicate line drawings and minimalist photography, the back-end operation is a masterclass in guerrilla logistics. Delivering physical artworks out of a country under heavy military bombardment and stringent international sanctions requires ingenuity bordering on subversion.

“The logistics of it – we thought about this ad nauseam,” Duran says with a weary laugh. “Currently, this matter is changing on an hourly basis. The sanctions obviously have been very disruptive.”

Initially, Continuum relied on two domestic courier services capable of flying artwork packages from Tehran to shipment hubs in Dubai and Istanbul, where international carriers could take over. But as geopolitical tensions soared, regional airspace closed and commercial flight paths dissolved.

Duran explains: “The flight connections through the UAE were cancelled so the couriers told us that UAE is off the table. But the second UAE comes off the table, they figure out another way. There is a man who had a courier company that was forced to shut down. In order to keep his business going, he is now using the ground borders, moving overland from Iran into Armenia. He goes by the land border, carries the artworks into Armenia and ships them out from there with full insurance.”

To manage expectations, Continuum informs international buyers that delivery may take three to six months. Yet collectors worldwide, ranging from private patrons in North America to major European institutions, have shown extraordinary patience.

For Duran, the real tragedy of the current crisis lies in the indiscriminate cruelty of international economic sanctions, which target ordinary citizens while doing nothing to alter political outcomes. “These sanctions are not putting much pressure on the government,” he observes. “It’s mostly punishing everybody that’s trying to live a life here. Everyone’s complaining but we’re trying to find solutions.”

A mong the artists trying to make a way out of no way is Mehrdad Jafari , 43, who grew up in the northern province of Mazandaran, where his relatives worked as sculptors and painters. Speaking from Tehran through a Farsi interpreter, he says: “Growing up, I always had the dream that one day I would be in Tehran and have an art studio in this city, to create work and fully realise my potential.

“My entire life has been dedicated, and continues to be dedicated, to my work. In fact, my existence is connected to my work. I have no other way of being. I must continue until I die.”

As the father of a three-year-old child, Jafari’s experience of the war is filtered through the anxieties of parenthood. His artwork, which centres on the complex emotional tapestry of human relationships and community interactions, has had to adapt to severe material deprivations.

“Because of the effect of sanctions, we’ve had to be a lot more imaginative in order to decide what materials we use,” Jafari explains. “Materials are quite difficult to find right now. But what I’ve had to do, and what others are doing, is replace this lack of materials with imagination. We use alternative materials to carry on.”

Jafari views this enforced improvisation as a double-edged sword. “In one way we use our imaginations more, creating a more creative space and ways of thinking. But on the other hand, of course, we would love to be part of the global system and have access to the things everybody else has access to. That’s just not available to us right now.”

For Jafari, Continuum’s launch during a time of active military conflict carries symbolic resonance. “It’s an extraordinary moment. It’s a bridge for us to connect with an international audience. For me personally, it brings a sense of calm – that we are not forgotten. Because of Continuum, I am more invigorated than ever to work. It gives us hope that life can carry on.”

From the outset, Duran and Rasti insisted that the initiative would not function as an exhibition about war, nor would it force artists to turn their pain into visual entertainment for foreign viewers.

Duran argues: “Iranian contemporary art doesn’t look like any one thing. Iran is not a style, and the Iranian identity is not a medium. An artist living in Shiraz shouldn’t have to make work that visually announces ‘Iran’ before an international audience is willing to take it seriously. We wanted the work to be encountered first as art, not as evidence about a country.”

While some participating artists choose to directly address conflict, Continuum refused to make political commentary or suffering a requirement for inclusion.

“There is a difference between giving artists visibility during a crisis and asking artists to make the crisis visible,” Duran adds. “I definitely didn’t want crisis to become the reason their work deserves attention. Context should deepen our understanding of an artwork; it shouldn’t imprison the artwork.”

The breadth of work included on the platform bears out this philosophy. Across 500 pieces, viewers encounter delicate geometric abstraction, haunting figurative portraiture, avant-garde photography, experimental printmaking and sculpture.

T he financial relief generated by Continuum is already providing vital support to Iran’s artistic ecosystem. In a country where currency devaluation has eroded savings, a single $500 artwork sale can provide significant income towards studio rent or much-needed pigments.

Issari, 38, reflects: “It creates a chain. If an artist is not so worried about their income, maybe they can continue teaching. If they can continue to teach, kids can continue to learn. The whole chain does not stop and we don’t fall into this pit of absolute hopelessness.”

Issari could not bring herself to work during the first weeks of heavy bombardment in Tehran. “I was here for the whole show. Hearing explosions five times, six times per day, every day – having to gather the cats and run to your safe place and count to 10. Then, as soon as it’s over, pick up the phone, check if your father is alive, if your mother’s alive, if your loved ones are OK. On repeat. It does a number on you.”

The trauma was physical as much as psychological. “I didn’t touch a brush,” she recalls. “Actually, I did once, and my hands were shaking so badly that I literally just put it down. I was like, ‘I am not going to do this right now.’ And that’s OK, because I’m just not there.”

While Issari, who studied art in London, is hopeful her paintings on Continuum will find homes in international collections, the initiative’s primary gift is emotional validation. “Even if you don’t sell, it’s that feeling of being seen,” she says with quiet determination. “For me, it’s tremendous. It’s easy to feel like you’re a pariah and you’re invisible. Just the fact that you’re being seen means a lot.”

She adds: “I always have faith in the fact that art will survive, regardless of everything and anything. Artists are the best. If problem-solving were an Olympic sport, we would win a gold medal every time. We will find a way.”

伊朗的库拉特和创始人杜兰艺术项目. 出生在希拉兹,但在加拿大长大,杜兰在摄影,艺术史和库拉托研究学位。 六年前,由诺斯塔利亚和与他的遗产联系的愿望驱动,他搬到伊朗,在那里他爱上了国内艺术场景的动态。", "links": [{"text": "Dario Duran", "url": "https://www.instagram.com/darioduran/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/d330d73fe38521adc2b1ffd932fb0e4bda4579bc/0_0_5000_4000/master/5000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "白色和黑色肖像 玛丽亚姆·拉斯蒂和达里奥·杜兰", "caption": "玛丽亚姆·拉斯蒂和达里奥·杜兰(Mariam Rasti and Dario Duran) 作曲:《继续的勇气:伊朗的艺术援助》", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当战争爆发时,杜兰发现自己直接被困在他的十字架上,“我被驱逐出境,”38岁的伊朗西拉兹解释道,“我妈妈和爸爸从加拿大访问,我们不得不逃离西拉兹,因为西拉兹每天都被打得很硬。", "links": [{"text": "Iran", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/world/iran"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在北方,杜兰遇到了数十名其他流离失所的文化工人,他们逃离了炸弹袭击的城市中心,如德黑兰和伊斯法汉,他与杜兰艺术项目的共同创始人玛丽亚姆·拉斯蒂联系在一起,他也逃离了首都。", "links": [{"text": "Mariam Rasti", "url": "https://www.instagram.com/mariamrasti/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我们一直在与艺术家沟通,”杜兰回忆道,“我们一次又一次看到的一件事是,像从未见过一样,艺术家失去了希望,展览被取消,画廊关闭,无法找到材料,艺术家被驱逐出境,每个人都经历了明天发生的事情的同样的不确定性。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我跑的当代艺术世界在一个结构泡沫内运行,隔离国际银行网络,通常,一个艺术家工作一年或两年,以准备一个工作体,依靠一个单一的画廊展览室,产生足够的销售,以生存下两年。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "杜兰说:“我们意识到,在这个时候,展览制作,治疗,档案 - 这些事情并不重要,重要的是,比其他任何东西,只是销售,这些艺术家无法支付租金。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“一位艺术家把他的绘画刷子和绘画管放在迪瓦尔(一个分类网站)上,只是为了继续下去,另一位艺术家告诉我:“我要去咖啡店工作,因为我不知道这件艺术事物是否会为我工作。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "决定做出差异,杜兰购买了一些吉加比特的互联网访问,以便他可以通过WhatsApp。从他的笔记本电脑在北方,他制定了一个开放的信给国际收藏家,博物馆导演和画家在整个隔离,放松了创作者在伊朗内部的麻烦。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "答案是即时的,令人惊叹的,伦敦,纽约,巴黎,迪拜,多伦多和孟买的画家和校长写了回来,渴望帮助。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "五个月的热情发展,杜兰,拉斯蒂和一联盟的国内画廊建造了Continuum. 数字平台聚集了超过500个原创艺术作品的200多名当代艺术家生活和工作在伊朗。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "伊朗11家商业画廊同意自愿辞职100其销售佣金的百分比. "起初,Continuum依靠两家国内航班服务,能够从德黑兰飞往迪拜和伊斯坦布尔的运输中心,但随着地缘政治紧张局势爆发,区域空域关闭,商业航班路线解散。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "杜兰解释说:“通过阿联酋的航班连接被取消,所以库尔人告诉我们,阿联酋在桌子上,但第二个阿联酋在桌子上,他们发现了另一种方式,有一位有一个库尔公司被迫关闭,为了保持他的业务,他现在使用地面边界,从伊朗转移到亚美尼亚,他走过地面边界,将艺术品带到亚美尼亚,并从那里发送他们全保险。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "为了管理期望,Continuum向国际买家报告,交付可能需要三到六个月,但全球收藏家,从北美的私人经纪人到主要的欧洲机构,表现出极大的耐心。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对于杜兰来说,当前危机的真正悲剧在于国际经济制裁的无歧视残酷性,针对普通公民,而不是为了改变政治结果而做任何事情,“这些制裁不会对政府施加太多的压力,”他指出,“这主要是惩罚所有试图在这里生活的人,每个人都在抱怨,但我们正在寻找解决方案。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "艺术家们试图从未走过路的一个小伙子是Mehrdad Jafari,43岁,在马桑达兰省北部长大,在那里他的亲戚作为雕塑家和画家工作。 通过一个法尔西翻译,他说:“长大,我总是梦想有一天我会在德黑兰,在这个城市有一个艺术工作室,创造工作,并充分实现我的潜力。", "links": [{"text": "Mehrdad Jafari", "url": {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/37e096c8b4c279c24c115a0468d46d9fda64324a/0_0_3024_4032/master/3024.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "抽象绘画", "caption": "作为一个三岁的孩子的父亲,贾法里的战争经验通过父母的焦虑被过滤,他的艺术作品,专注于人际关系和社区互动的复杂情感背景,不得不适应严重的物质剥夺。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“由于制裁的影响,我们不得不更具想象力来决定我们使用哪些材料,”Jafari解释道,“材料现在很难找到,但我不得不做的事情和其他人正在做的事情就是用想象力取代这种缺乏材料,我们使用替代材料来进行。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "贾法里认为这种强迫的 improvisation 是一种双重的剑:“一方面,我们使用我们的想象力更多,创造更多的创造空间和思维方式,但另一方面,当然,我们会喜欢成为全球体系的一部分,并获得其他每个人都可以访问的东西,这只是现在不适合我们。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "对于Jafari来说,在积极的军事冲突时期,Continuum的启动具有象征性的响应:“这是一个非凡的时刻,这是我们与国际观众联系的桥梁,对我个人来说,它带来了平静的感觉,我们不会被遗忘,因为Continuum,我比以往任何时候都更有兴奋,希望生活能继续下去。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "从一开始,杜兰和拉斯蒂坚持,该举措不会作为关于战争的展览,也不会强迫艺术家将他们的痛苦转化为外国观众的视觉娱乐。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "杜兰说:“伊朗当代艺术看起来不像任何东西,伊朗不是风格,伊朗的身份不是媒体,居住在希拉兹的艺术家不应该做一个视觉宣布“伊朗”的工作,而国际观众愿意认真对待它,我们希望这项工作首先作为艺术,而不是作为一个国家的证据。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "虽然一些参与的艺术家选择直接解决冲突,但Continuum拒绝发表政治评论或遭受参与的要求。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“在危机期间给予艺术家可见性和要求艺术家让危机可见之间存在差异,”杜兰补充道,“我绝对不想危机成为他们的作品值得关注的原因。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "该平台上包含的作品的宽度引发了这个哲学,大约有500件作品,观众会遇到微妙的地质抽象,寻找形象肖像,前卫摄影,实验印刷和雕塑。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "由Continuum产生的财务援助已经为伊朗艺术生态系统提供了重要支持,在货币贬值破坏了储蓄的国家,单一500美元的艺术作品销售可以为工作室租赁或非常需要的色素提供显著的收入。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "38岁的伊萨里说:“它创造了一个链条,如果一个艺术家对他们的收入不那么担心,也许他们可以继续教学,如果他们可以继续教学,孩子们可以继续学习,整个链条不会停止,我们不会陷入绝对绝望的陷阱。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": translated_title_zh: “我必须继续,直到我死去”:在伊朗蓬勃发展的艺术场景带到世界的斗争中
translated_excerpt_zh: 在经济制裁和持续冲突之间,一个新的举措是将伊朗艺术家带回国际光明,当电话早上到来时,德黑兰居民伊萨里知道必须紧急。

title_original: Beer With a Painter: Melissa Brown

editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "访谈", "links": [{"text": "Interview", "url": "https://hyperallergic.com/tag/interview/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "与画家共饮啤酒：梅丽莎·布朗", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我想具象化这样一个事实：尽管我们的感知如此，但现实是可变的，”这位常驻布鲁克林的艺术家在谈到自己的画作时说道。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://storage.ghost.io/c/51/f8/51f871d8-b6be-4a73-b958-0ca4fff0110a/content/images/size/w1200/2026/10/Melissa-Brown-2-modified.jpg", "alt": "与画家共饮啤酒：梅丽莎·布朗", "caption": "", "credit": "Hyperallergic", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Hyperallergic；其余所有照片由 Adam Reich 拍摄，艺术家惠允）", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "梅丽莎·布朗（Melissa Brown）自青少年时期以来，每天都画着猫眼妆。我不禁将它与她的画作联系起来：在那些画中，神圣与世俗在镜面、店铺橱窗、灵媒桌椅和卧室祭坛之间交汇。猫眼眼线极具戏剧张力且充满力量，可追溯至古埃及，当时女性使用矿物眼线是为了健康功效以及抵御邪眼。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "为了暗喻我们日常体验的层层叠叠，布朗将多种技术融为一体：摄影、外光派绘画、CMYK 印刷、喷枪和模板。有时她的画作还附带二维码，可将观众引导至一段动画。她的画作《Commute》（2020）描绘了一只留着长指甲、贴着穿戴甲的手，在一个空无一人的疫情时期地铁车厢里转动着闪亮的冥想球，车厢正驶过布鲁克林大桥，窗外隐约可见一个发光的太阳圆球。绘制的频闪效果让手指和反光球产生动感——这是对英国漩涡主义画家西比尔·安德鲁斯（Sybil Andrews）的致敬。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://storage.ghost.io/c/51/f8/51f871d8-b6be-4a73-b958-0ca4fff0110a/content/images/2026/10/Commute.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Hyperallergic", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "布朗的工作室位于布鲁克林弗拉特布什（Flatbush）一栋建筑的二楼，楼下是一家热闹的熟食店，楼上是一家编发沙龙。造访这里的体验有点像走进了她的画作，在玻璃店铺橱窗后，日常生活的琐碎与美丽仪式的表演性元素相互碰撞。上个月，我们在那里见面，聊起了她最喜欢的文艺复兴时期画作、在城市漫步时偶遇母题的魔力、在漂浮物中寻找答案，以及绘画如何将体验具象化。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "梅丽莎·布朗于1974年出生于新泽西州莫里斯敦，在罗德岛设计学院（RISD）获得版画专业美术学士学位（BFA），在耶鲁大学获得绘画与版画专业美术硕士学位（MFA）。布朗还于2000年就读于斯考希根绘画与雕塑学校（Skowhegan School of Painting and Sculpture）。她目前是纽约市立大学雷曼学院（Lehman College）的教授，并联合策展了双场地群展《这味道正常吗？当代艺术中的幽默》（Does This Taste Funny? Humor in Contemporary Art），该展在雷曼学院美术馆（Lehman College Art Gallery）以及莎拉劳伦斯学院海姆博尔德视觉艺术中心画廊（Gallery at Heimbold Visual Arts Center at Sarah Lawrence College）展出。布朗近期的个展《Window Shopping》在纽约德里克·埃勒画廊（Derek Eller Gallery）举办，自2017年起她便在该画廊参展。", "links": [{"text": "Does This Taste Funny? Humor in Contemporary Art", "url": "https://www.lehmangallery.org/current-exhibition?ref=hyperallergic.com"}, {"text": "Window Shopping", "url": "https://www.derekeller.com/exhibitions/melissa-brown4?ref=hyperallergic.com"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Hyperallergic：你年轻时是如何接触到艺术的，又是什么引领你进入罗德岛设计学院（RISD）的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "梅丽莎·布朗：我出生在新泽西州，我的家人都在那里，但我是在费城附近长大的。当我的父母最初从新泽西搬到费城时，我们在中心城（Center City）租了一套公寓，靠近本杰明·富兰克林博物馆（Ben Franklin Museum）。该馆最近为美国建国二百周年进行了翻新。那里有一个带有许多霓虹灯的无限镜面房间，还有一个互动房间，里面有电话，你可以拿起来听听历史人物的声音。还有一个玻璃口琴。小时候，我经常吵着要去那里，我妈妈就会带我去。我甚至有一段时间想改名叫“本杰明·富兰克林”。我们无数次参观了他的印刷作坊。这一定对我有影响。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "到了参观大学的时候，其中一所就是罗德岛设计学院。我被它迷住了，这是决定性的因素。我走进他们的伍兹-格里画廊（Woods-Gerry Gallery），觉得这就是我想待的地方。", "translated": true}]

article_text:
Interview

Beer With a Painter: Melissa Brown

“I want to visualize the fact that, despite our perception, reality is changeable,” the Brooklyn-based artist said of her paintings.

Hyperallergic ; all other photos Adam Reich, courtesy the artist)

Melissa Brown has worn cat-eye makeup every day since she was a teenager. I can’t help but associate it with her paintings, where the sacred and profane converge amid mirrored surfaces, shop windows, psychics’ tables, and bedroom altars. The cat-eye flick is dramatic and powerful, dating back to ancient Egypt, where women wore mineral liner for its health properties and as protection against the evil eye.

To connote the layering of our daily experience, Brown collages a spectrum of techniques: photography, plein-air painting, CMYK printing, airbrush, and stencil. Sometimes her paintings come with QR codes that send the viewer to an animation. Her painting “Commute” (2020) shows a hand with long fingers and press-on nails spinning shiny meditation balls in an otherwise empty pandemic-era subway car passing in front of the Brooklyn Bridge, a glowing orb of sunlight visible through the window. A painted strobe effect animates the fingers and the reflective balls — a nod to British Vorticist painter Sybil Andrews.

Brown’s studio is on the second floor of a building in Flatbush, Brooklyn, with a busy deli in the storefront and a braiding salon upstairs. The experience of visiting is a bit like walking into one of her paintings, where the mundane and the performative elements of beauty rituals collide through glass shop windows. Last month, we met there to talk about her favorite Renaissance painting, the magic of encountering motifs while walking around the city, finding answers in flotsam, and how paintings can manifest experience.

Melissa Brown was born in 1974 in Morristown, New Jersey, and received her BFA in Printmaking from the Rhode Island School of Design (RISD) and her MFA in Painting and Printmaking from Yale University. Brown also attended the Skowhegan School of Painting and Sculpture in 2000. She is currently a professor at Lehman College of the City University of New York and co-curated a two-venue group exhibition, Does This Taste Funny? Humor in Contemporary Art , on view at Lehman College Art Gallery and the Gallery at Heimbold Visual Arts Center at Sarah Lawrence College. Brown’s recent solo exhibition, Window Shopping , was presented in New York at Derek Eller Gallery, where she has exhibited since 2017.

Hyperallergic: How did you connect with art as a young person, and what brought you to RISD?

Melissa Brown: I was born in New Jersey, where all of my family is from, but I grew up near Philadelphia. When my parents first moved from New Jersey to Philadelphia, we had an apartment in Center City, near the Ben Franklin Museum. It had recently been updated for the Bicentennial. There was an infinity mirror room with a lot of neon, and an interactive room with phones that you could pick up and listen to someone from history. There was also a glass harmonica. As a child, I was constantly asking to go there and my mom would take me. I even went through a phase where I wanted to be called “Ben Franklin.” We visited his print shop a million times. It must have had an influence.

When it came time to visit colleges, one of them was RISD. I was seduced by it, and that was the determining factor. I went into their Woods-Gerry Gallery and felt it was where I wanted to be.

editorial_title_zh: 吉尔玛切夫·盖特内特：人类之圈 / “我因我们而在”

{"type": "paragraph", "text": "“从艺术和科学的角度来看，所有人类都属于同一个物种，即智人，且几乎共享相同的DNA。尽管有着这一共同的生物学基础，世界各地的人们却生活在众多不同的语言、传统和生活方式之中。我通过融合色彩，将所有这些汇聚在一起。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "人类之圈 / "在这场展览中，“人类之圈”通过从具体物体向纯粹形式的过渡，同时体现了现实主义与抽象主义。色彩的融合将这两个概念统一起来。在本次展览中，我将大幅具象艺术作品与抽象作品并置呈现。我认为这是一个绝佳的机会，能够通过“人类之圈”这一统一的主题来凸显对比，展现两种截然不同的艺术形式，并彰显我艺术涉猎的广度。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "+", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“人类之圈”——或称“人类——圆圈”——的概念是一个强有力、包容性极强的愿景，它聚焦于所有人之间的团结、联系和平等，无论其肤色、宗教、种族、性取向或背景如何。它象征着一个平等者的聚会，通常被称为“安全空间”，每个人都被邀请在这里分享他们独特的经历。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "+", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "圆圈代表了对人性的“360度”视角，有意将所有人以及所有身份汇聚在一个共享的空间里。围成一圈消除了等级制度。不同于教室或剧院等传统的线性排列，圆圈能让每个人都看到并听到彼此，从而促进联系和真实的沟通。对圆圈的许多解读都强调了从过时、分裂和父权制的权力结构向更加平等的“人类共同体”的过渡。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "+", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“乌班图”（Ubuntu）这一概念大致翻译自祖鲁语，意为“我因我们而在”，它根植于同名的非洲哲学，强调人们是通过与他人的联系来寻找自我身份和生活目标的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://africanah.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Get1-300x223.jpg", "alt": "Get1", "caption": "", "credit": "Africanah.org", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://africanah.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Get2-300x227.jpg", "alt": "Get2", "caption": "", "credit": "Africanah.org", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "对话吉尔玛切夫·盖特内特（GIRMACHEW GETNET）：10个问题", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "■ 你如何定义自己如今的核心艺术之声或风格？", "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "我的艺术风格反映了一种多面向的视觉叙事。将不同的时代和面孔融合在一起，就像在画布上混合色彩一样。它表明，所有时代的人们都拥有同样的心灵和灵魂。我的概念将人类历史描绘成一个大家庭。新旧交融为一个统一的整体，而融合历史类似于在抽象绘画中使用新技术。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "■ 是哪些核心主题或文化对话推动着你目前的一系列作品？", "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "全球混乱的状态，以及各种冲突和战争，促使我通过创作这些大型抽象艺术作品来探索实现内心平静的概念。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "■ 你的现代风格是如何从你早期的项目中演变而来的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "我早期的艺术作品大多是具象的。这是我的首次个展，全部由大幅抽象画作组成。这种媒介使我能够比用现实主义绘画更有效地表达想法，特别是对于这次名为“人类——圆圈”的展览而言。作为一名自由艺术家，我有机会和能力通过各种媒介和风格来表达我的想法。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://africanah.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Get3-300x223.jpg", "alt": "Get3", "caption": "", "credit": "Africanah.org", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://africanah.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Get4-300x227.jpg", "alt": "Get4", "caption": "", "credit": "Africanah.org", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "■ 当观众第一次接触你的艺术时，你希望他们感受到什么或思考什么？", "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "艺术由视觉元素组成，所以我建议来到我展览的参观者相信自己的眼睛，并吸收画作传达的信息。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "■ 你如何将无形的概念或情感转化为非具象的形式？在当今饱和的视觉景观中，“现代抽象”对你而言意味着什么？", "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "由于没有清晰的图像可看，观众会将他们自己的故事带入艺术中。这一切都取决于你如何看待和理解它——而这正是艺术如此特别的原因所在。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "■ 你的成品创作中有多少是受严格的内在逻辑驱动的，又有多少是源于未经计算的原始直觉？在你的色域和手势笔触背后，是否有特定的社会政治、建筑或心理学主题？", "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "在工作室里，这些大幅抽象画作的诞生相当自发，没有犹豫或迟疑。有时是有计划的，有时则不然；它们背后没有隐藏的动机、策略或意图。这纯粹是将秩序与无序融合在一起的过程。在这一过程中，它完全依赖于先天本能，而不是习得或排练过的行为。它是纯粹而自由的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "■ 你是如何知道一件艺术品已经完全完成的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "我的艺术品永远不会真正完成——只要它们还在工作室里，我就会定期对它们进行加工，添加图层。这并不意味着我抛弃它们——我从不抛弃艺术品，而是让它们焕发新生。我继续创作这些作品，一步步赋予它们生命，就像我们一样——随着时间推移，它们会生长和变化。因此，我的工作室成了一个充满无限生命力的地方。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "■ 你来自哪里，你的环境是如何塑造你的风格的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "■ 我来自埃塞俄比亚，但我的艺术是普世的。我在美因河畔法兰克福生活了很多年，在这里找到了家的感觉，这是一个在许多方面都堪称欧洲心脏的多元文化城市。法兰克福来自世界各地的专业人士的多样性，帮助我进一步发展了关于激励人心的理想人类环境的想法。我在埃塞俄比亚和非洲的童年与背景塑造了我独特的创作之声，而我在法兰克福和欧洲的生活经历以及这座城市的多元文化精神则激发了我日常的工作。在全球社群中结识来自世界各地的人们，帮助我进一步发展了我的“人类之圈”理念。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "■ 你如何在艺术的商业一面与纯粹的创造力之间保持平衡？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "作为艺术家，我们的工作是进行创造并发展构思，而不是专注于商业。但艺术与艺术商业有着相同的创作核心，因为艺术的创作与销售都依赖于新点子。艺术家根据愿景创作作品，而艺术企业家则带着同样的精神开拓市场。这两个领域都需要想象力才能发展。因此，艺术家和艺术经纪人是同一枚硬币的两面。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": article_text:
“From both an artistic and a scientific perspective, all humans belong to a single species, Homo sapiens, and share almost the same DNA. Despite this common biological basis, people around the world live with many different languages, traditions and ways of life. I bring all of these together by blending colours.”

Circle – Humans / ‘I Am Because We Are’

About the exhibition:

In this exhibition, ‘Circle – Humans’ embodies both realism and abstraction by transitioning from concrete objects to pure form. The blending of colours unites these two concepts. In this exhibition, I present my large-format figurative art works alongside my abstract pieces. I see this as a wonderful opportunity to highlight contrasts, using the unifying theme of ‘Circle – Humans’ to showcase two distinct art forms and demonstrate the breadth of my artistic range.

+

The concept of ‘Circle – Humans’ – or ‘Human – Circle’ – is a powerful, inclusive vision that focuses on unity, connectedness, and equality among all people, regardless of skin colour, religion, ethnicity, sexual orientation, or background. It symbolises a gathering of equals, often referred to as a ‘safe space’, where everyone is invited to share their unique experiences.

+

The circle represents a ‘360-degree’ view of humanity, deliberately bringing all people and all identities together in a shared space. Gathering in a circle eliminates hierarchies. Unlike traditional linear arrangements, such as in classrooms or theatres, a circle enables everyone to see and hear each other, thereby fostering connection and authentic communication. Many interpretations of the circle emphasise a transition from outdated, divisive and patriarchal power structures to a more egalitarian ‘community of humanity’.

+

The concept of ‘Ubuntu’, which translates roughly from the Zulu language as ‘I am because we are’, has its roots in an African philosophy of the same name and emphasises that people find their identity and purpose in life through their connection with others.

10 questions with GIRMACHEW GETNET

■ How would you define your core artistic voice or style today?

My artistic style reflects a multifaceted visual narrative. Fusing different eras and faces is like mixing colours on a canvas. It shows that people across all eras share the same heart and soul. My concept portrays human history as one big family. The old and the new merge into a unified whole, and blending history is similar to using new techniques in abstract painting.

■ What core themes or cultural conversations drive your current body of work?

The state of global chaos, as well as the various conflicts and wars, has led me to explore the concept of achieving inner peace through creating these large-scale abstract artworks.

■ How has your modern style evolved from your earlier projects?

Most of my earlier artworks are figurative. This is my first solo exhibition, consisting exclusively of large-format abstract paintings. This medium enables me to express ideas more effectively than I could with realistic paintings, particularly for this exhibition, ‘Human – Circle’. As a freelance artist, I have the opportunity and ability to express my ideas through various media and styles.

■ What do you want viewers to feel or think when they encounter your art for the first time?

Art consists of visual elements, so I advise visitors to my exhibition to trust their eyes and take in the information conveyed by the paintings.

■ How do you translate intangible concepts or emotions into non-representational forms? What does ‘modern abstraction’ mean to you in today’s saturated visual landscape?

Since there is no clear image to look at, viewers bring their own stories to the art. It all depends on how you see and understand it — and that is precisely what makes art so special.

■ How much of your finished work is driven by strict internal logic versus raw, uncalculated instinct? Are there specific socio-political, architectural or psychological themes underpinning your colour fields and gestural marks?

In the studio, these large-format abstract paintings emerge quite spontaneously, without hesitation or delay. Sometimes it is planned and sometimes it is not; there is no hidden motif, strategy or intention behind them. It is simply a matter of merging the orderly and the disorderly together. In doing so, the process relies exclusively on innate nature, not learned or rehearsed behaviour. It is pure and free.

■ How do you know when a piece of artwork is completely finished?

My artworks are never finished — as long as they’re in the studio, I work on them periodically, adding layers. That doesn’t mean I discard them – I never discard artworks, but rather renew them. I continue to work on the pieces, bringing them to life step by step, just like us — they grow and change over time. My studio thus becomes a place of infinite life.

■ Where are you from, and how does your environment shape your style?

■ I’m from Ethiopia, but my art is universal. I have lived in Frankfurt am Main for many years and feel at home here, in a multicultural city that is, in many ways, the heart of Europe. The diversity of professionals from all over the world in Frankfurt helps me to further develop the idea of a motivating human environment.My childhood and background in Ethiopia and Africa shape my unique creative voice, while my life experiences in Frankfurt and Europe, as well as the city’s multicultural spirit, inspire my daily work. Meeting people from all over the world in the global community helps me further develop my Circle – Humans ideas.

■ How do you balance the business side of art with pure creativity?

As artists, it is our job to be creative and develop ideas, not to focus on business. But art and the art business share the same creative focus because the creation and sale of art both depend on new ideas. An artist creates a work based on a vision, and an art entrepreneur taps into a market with that same spirit. Both fields require imagination to grow. Artists and art dealers are therefore two sides of the same coin.

■What upcoming projects or exhibitions are you most excited about?

We’ll figure it out together.

Interview: Galyna Gubriienko, an art curator student from Ukraine., interview will be published in mid-September in the newspaper MONTEZ.

article_text:
Neues Thema für die Met-Gala, die Art Basel Paris als Laufsteg und eine Art Cologne mit Bodenhaftung: Das ist unsere Medienschau am Freitag

Documenta

Zwei anonyme Künstlerinnen oder Künstler der Documenta 15 geben in "Hyperallergic" eingeladenen Teilnehmenden der kommenden Ausgabe zynische Ratschläge und zeichnen ihr Kasseler Erlebnis als Horrortrip. Sie berichten, wie sie nach ihrer Teilnahme massiven Antisemitismusvorwürfen, Medienkampagnen und Angriffen ausgesetzt gewesen seien – mit Folgen für ihre Karrieren und ihre psychische Gesundheit. Die deutsche Kulturpolitik habe sich als abhängig von staatlichen Vorgaben erwiesen, die Institution Documenta ihre Künstler nicht ausreichend geschützt. "Die Institution wird zuerst sich selbst gegen jeden Angriff oder Vorwurf verteidigen", warnen die Autoren. Wer teilnehme, solle deshalb vorab schriftliche Schutz- und Kommunikationszusagen der Leitung verlangen, die Haltung des Kuratorenteams zu Palästina klären und sich früh mit den anderen Künstlern vernetzen. Am Ende müsse jede Entscheidung dazu beitragen, den Krieg in Gaza zu beenden, nicht die Institution zu legitimieren.

Museen

Die "New York Times" berichtet über das neue Thema der Met-Gala und der begleitenden Kostümausstellung 2027 : Statt einer ursprünglich geplanten Schau über John Galliano, die nach Protesten wegen seiner antisemitischen Äußerungen abgesagt wurde , widmet sich das Costume Institute nun der Alltagskleidung. Unter dem Titel "extraOrdinary: Fashion and the Poetics of the Everyday" sollen Jeans, T-Shirts und Daunenjacken im Kontext der Haute Couture gezeigt werden. Kurator Andrew Bolton betont, die Ausstellung solle Fragen nach Konsum, Ressourcen und Wertvorstellungen aufwerfen. Dabei sei ihm bewusst, dass die modische Aneignung einfacher Kleidung auch soziale Spannungen berühre. Sein Wunsch: Besucher sollten ihre eigene Garderobe anschließend mit anderen Augen betrachten.

Kunstmarkt

Michael Kohler berichtet in der "Kölnischen Rundschau" von einer Art Cologne zwischen Bodenständigkeit und Luxusanspruch. Während Messechef Daniel Hug einen Jaguar am Eingang platziert habe, stellte Kulturstaatsminister Wolfram Weimer Unterstützung des Bundes in Aussicht . Der Galerienverband wirbt unterdessen für einen staatlichen Galeriepreis. Die neue "Private Preview" am Mittwochnachmittag sei gut besucht gewesen, habe sich aber nicht als "Gamechanger" erwiesen. Insgesamt bleibe die Messe ein "normaler Markt für normale Menschen" und ein Treffpunkt für den harten Kern der Kunstliebhaber.

Elisa Carollo beobachtet im "Observer" , dass die Kunstwelt trotz des ungelösten Konflikts mit dem Iran verstärkt auf den Golf als Kunstmarkt setzt. Christie’s erzielte bei seiner ersten Auktion in Abu Dhabi Anfang November knapp neun Millionen Dollar; mehr als 30 Prozent der Bieter waren jünger als 40 Jahre. Auch Sotheby’s baut seine Präsenz in der Region aus und plant weitere Auktionen in Abu Dhabi, während Frieze im November erstmals eine Messe in der Stadt veranstaltet. Im Dezember soll zudem das Guggenheim Abu Dhabi eröffnen. Art Basel bereitet unterdessen die zweite Ausgabe ihrer Messe in Katar für Januar 2027 vor. Die Veranstalter betonen, die geopolitische Lage genau zu beobachten, halten aber an ihren Expansionsplänen fest.

Vincent Noce berichtet im "The Art Newspaper" über Betrugsvorwürfe im Zusammenhang mit Picasso-Silberarbeiten und Goldmedaillons . Die Familie des Künstlers habe im März Strafanzeige wegen Betrugs, Fälschung und unerlaubter Reproduktionen erstattet. Nach Angaben der Picasso-Verwaltung seien mindestens 17 verdächtige Sammlungen mit Hunderten Objekten aufgetaucht. Offenbar seien Gussformen aus der Werkstatt Ateliers Hugo für nicht autorisierte Neuauflagen verwendet worden. Das australische Museum of Old and New Art hatte bereits 2023 Zweifel an einem bei Sotheby’s für 1,4 Millionen Pfund versteigerten Picasso-Teller-Set geäußert. Auch Bonhams sagte eine Auktion mit Arbeiten aus der Werkstatt ab. Nicolas Hugo, Enkel des Firmengründers, bestreitet, selbst Picasso-Arbeiten reproduziert zu haben. Die Ermittlungen stehen noch am Anfang. Zugleich steckt das traditionsreiche Atelier in einer Krise: Nach dem Tod seines Vaters 2023 lehnten dessen fünf Kinder das Erbe ab.

Liam Freeman stellt im "New York Magazine" die Menschen vor, die während der Art Basel Paris im Grand Palais unterwegs waren – kurz bevor Proteste die Messe zur vorzeitigen Schließung zwangen. In der Fotostrecke erzählen Künstler, Galeristen, Sammler und Kunsttechniker von ihren Eindrücken. Ein Kunsttransporteur aus Berlin beschreibt etwa, wie er seine Haarfarbe auf sein Outfit abstimme; ein Galerist aus Abidjan berichtet von seinem Bedürfnis, mit einem farbigen Schal aus der schwarzen Arbeitskleidung herauszustechen. Der Künstler Rodrigue Fondeviolle sieht in den Protesten eine Konfrontation mit der Wirklichkeit: Die Kunstwelt schotte sich mit ihren weißen Galerieräumen oft von gesellschaftlichen Konflikten ab, während der kommerzielle Betrieb politische Botschaften entschärfe. Auch Klaus Biesenbach spricht von einer Reise zwischen Protesten und Sorge um Europa – und schwärmt zugleich von der kulturellen Vielfalt der Pariser Kunstszene.

Gedenkkultur

Zahlreiche Menschen im US-Bundesstaat Minnesota haben Berichten zufolge am Tag der Kongresswahlen Aufkleber mit der Aufschrift "I voted" ("ich habe gewählt") an den Gedenkstätten für Renee Good und Alex Pretti angebracht. US-Medien veröffentlichten Fotos der bunt beklebten Erinnerungsorte für die beiden US-Bürger, die im Januar in Minneapolis bei Einsätzen der Einwanderungsbehörde ICE erschossen worden waren. "Wir können nicht ändern, was geschehen ist, aber wir werden weiterkämpfen", sagte eine Frau an der Gedenkstätte von Pretti dem Lokalsender Kare 11 . Sie habe den Sticker hinterlassen, "weil Alex nicht wählen durfte", sagte die Frau unter Tränen, "und weil es wirklich wichtig ist, dass wir unseren Stimmen Gehör verschaffen können". An einem Denkmal für die getötete Good sagte eine Frau dem Sender: "Ich möchte glauben, dass ihr Leben nicht umsonst war, dass sie zumindest zu einem Ankerpunkt geworden ist, der die Menschen mobilisiert und uns dazu bewegt hat, wählen zu gehen." Er habe bei den Gedenkstätten für Good und Pretti Halt gemacht, schrieb auch Minnesotas demokratischer Gouverneur Tim Walz auf der Plattform X . Er sei beeindruckt gewesen, wie viele Menschen dort ihre Anteilnahme bekundet und einen Sticker hinterlassen hätten. "Wir haben nicht vergessen", schrieb Walz. Die Verantwortlichen würden bald zur Rechenschaft gezogen. Der Frage, was die Midterms-Wahlen für die US-Kultur bedeuten, ist Quincy Mackay für Monopol International nachgegangen.

article_text:
３人の代表作の展示でテンション最高潮

国立新美術館(東京・六本木)で始まった「少女漫画・インフィニティ 萩尾望都×山岸凉子×大和和紀 三人展」。開幕前日の内覧会で取材しました。 三人の巨匠の代表作を大スケールで紹介するイントロダクションでテンションが一気に上がります。終盤まで息をつく暇もない、怒涛の展示です。巡回は予定されていません。

「はいからさん」「あさきゆめみし」 大和先生

少女漫画の世界に独創的なテーマと斬新な表現を取り入れ、漫画史に燦然と輝く３人です。デビューから現在に至る創作の軌跡を800点以上の原画などでたどります。 大和和紀先生といえば映像や舞台にもなった「はいからさんが通る」「あさきゆめみし」…。自立した女性像を鮮やかに描きました。

「ポーの一族」「トーマの心臓」 萩尾先生

「ポーの一族」「トーマの心臓」「11人いる！」など繊細な心理描写と壮大な世界観で読者を虜にした萩尾望都先生。こちらでも宝塚の舞台衣装が間近で見られます。

「日出処の天子」など衝撃作の数々、山岸先生

「アラベスク」「テレプシコーラ／舞姫」の鮮烈なバレエ漫画や、圧倒的な聖徳太子像の「日出処の天子」など、名作の数々で社会に衝撃を与えた山岸凉子先生。 原画で発表当時のインパクトが生々しく蘇ります。

国立美術館で初の少女漫画展、歴史的な一歩

国立の美術館で開催される初の大規模な少女漫画展です。その歴史的な一歩に相応しいレジェンドたちの夢の共演。

article_text:
Producers behind Hayakawa Chie’s Cannes competition title “ Renoir ” are among the speakers at a session on Asia-Europe co-production at Tokyo’s TIFFCOM market on Oct. 30, as Japanese accelerator Atmovie Global Track formalizes a partnership with Europe-based workshop Ties That Bind.

The open panel, titled “Building Creative Partnerships,” will examine how producers and directors work together to bring projects up to an international level, drawing on case studies of films made between the two regions. It will run in tandem with the Tokyo International Film Festival , and any TIFFCOM badge holder can attend.

Related Stories

Taylor Swift Fires Up Academy Gala With Four Songs in Her First Band Performance Since the Eras Tour

On the panel are Mizuno-Gray Eiko, CEO of Tokyo-based Loaded Films, and French producer Christophe Bruncher of Ici et Là Productions, who both worked on “Renoir,” which competed at Cannes in 2025. Mizuno-Gray’s credits also include Hayakawa’s “Plan 75,” which received a special mention for the Caméra d’Or at Cannes in 2022 and went on to become Japan’s Oscar entry, as well as Kurosawa Kiyoshi’s “To the Ends of the Earth.” She is developing a Poland-Japan co-production from director Ishikawa Kei and a Japan-Philippines project from Hirayanagi Atsuko, and is also a support producer on the accelerator. She also sits on the Tokyo festival’s Asian Future jury this year.

Popular on Variety

Bruncher, a La Fémis graduate who speaks Mandarin, is head of studies for Ties That Bind. His recent co-productions include Muriel d’Ansembourg’s Berlinale title “Truly Naked” and Kamila Andini’s Toronto selection “Four Seasons in Java,” both of which feature at this year’s Tokyo festival.

Joining them are Oh Heejung, the Seoul- and Amsterdam-based founder of Seesaw Pictures, whose films have played Sundance, Berlin, Locarno, IDFA, Rotterdam and Busan, and Moriya Takeshi, the Atmovie CEO who founded the accelerator. Moriya’s producing credits span TV series “Midnight Diner” and Uchida Eiji’s “Midnight Swan,” which was named picture of the year at the 44th Japan Academy Film Prizes. Atmovie Global Track producer Sekiguchi Mio, whose credits include Uchida’s “Fiamma,” curated the panel.

Ahead of the public event, Oh and Bruncher will mentor a closed two-day workshop for the accelerator’s fellows on Oct. 27 and 28, built around group sessions in which participants will develop their projects and discuss career paths rather than sit through lectures.

The overall program was curated by Alessandro Gropplero, who runs the Friuli Venezia Giulia Audiovisual Fund and co-founded Ties That Bind, which the FVG fund organizes with EAVE and the Udine Far East Film Festival. The workshop brings European and Asian producers together on project development, financing, co-production opportunities and networking.

Atmovie Global Track prepares Japanese filmmakers to take original projects into the international co-production market through lectures and mentoring from Japanese and overseas industry figures. Selected fellows pitch at festivals, with milestones including the Japan Pavilion at Cannes in May 2025 and the Japan Pitch event at the Busan International Film Festival in October. The organizers said many creators struggle to build trust across cultures and to communicate outside their native language, and that the open session is meant to share lessons with the wider industry and grow the network of Japanese filmmakers pursuing international work.

Support for the program comes from the Japan Creator Support Fund, which the Japan Arts Council created using Agency for Cultural Affairs funding.

title_original: Da cosa nasce cosa: l’atelier come spazio collettivo alla Fondazione Bevilacqua La Masa
editorial_title_zh: 事生于事：贝维拉夸·拉马萨基金会的集体空间工作室
editorial_excerpt_zh: 贝维拉夸·拉马萨基金会2025-2026年度工作室的总结展“事生于事”（Da cosa nasce cosa）目前正在威尼斯展出，将持续至11月22日。该展将工作室还原为相遇与实验的空间，勾勒出一个正在成型的艺术现场的地理图景。文章来自Da…
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "丹尼尔·布伦（Daniel Buren）在1971年出版的《工作室的功能》（The Function of the Studio）中写道：“工作室是第一个画框，是所有后续画框和限制条件赖以存在的第一个限制。”布伦将工作室视为一种预先决定所有展览的上层建筑：这是一个封闭的意识形态空间，他称之为“象牙塔”，艺术品在其中作为独立对象成型，然后才交付给展陈空间。他的艺术实践倾向于体制批判，反抗工作室的意识形态封闭性，表现为激进的特定场域（in situ）体验，与其所处的环境及环绕的各种关系密不可分。然而，布伦的范式仍然假定了一个内与外、一个需要声讨的围场。但是，当工作室本身变成一个多孔且具渗透性的空间、一个内部与外部之间的间隙场所，其中的艺术品自治被过程、关系、交流的暂时性以及相遇所取代时，这种对立还剩下什么？这就是象牙塔的倒塌：在其废墟之上，如今孕育出了一片能取代确定性与自治、带来可能与集体的萌芽之地。正是在这种开放且无界的（unbound）工作室视野之中，我们得以解读威尼斯贝维拉夸·拉马萨基金会2025-2026年度工作室的经历，该经历在由卡米拉·莫扎托（Camilla {"type": "paragraph", "text": "贝维拉夸·拉马萨基金会自1898年起便一直致力于支持新一代艺术家，威尼斯卡佩萨罗（Ca’Pesaro）在20世纪的经历便是明证，该地多年来一直是威尼斯当代艺术现场的展陈空间与孵化器。如今，借助与威尼斯市民博物馆基金会（Fondazione Musei Civici di article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Daniel Buren nel 1971, in The Function of the Studio scrive: «Lo studio è la prima cornice, il primo limite da cui dipenderanno tutte le cornici e i limiti successivi». Buren individua nell’atelier quella sovrastruttura che predetermina ogni esposizione: uno spazio chiuso e ideologico, da lui definito “torre d’avorio” in cui l’opera si costituisce come oggetto autonomo prima di essere consegnata allo spazio espositivo. La sua pratica artistica, orientata verso una critica istituzionale, si ribella alla chiusura ideologica dell’atelier, esplicitandosi in esperienze radicali in situ , indissociabili dal contesto che le ospita e dalle relazioni che le contornano. Il paradigma bureniano presuppone tuttavia ancora un dentro e un fuori, un recinto da denunciare. Ma cosa rimane di questa opposizione quando è l’atelier stesso a divenire uno spazio poroso e permeabile, un luogo interstiziale tra l’interno e l’esterno, in cui all’autonomia dell’opera si sostituisce il processo, la relazione, la provvisorietà dello scambio, l’incontro? È l’abbattimento della torre d’avorio: su di essa nasce, ora, un terreno germinativo che sostituisce al certo, il possibile e all’autonomo, il collettivo. È entro questo orizzonte di uno studio aperto e unbound , che si può leggere l’esperienza degli Atelier 2025-2026 della Fondazione Bevilacqua La Masa di Venezia, restituita nella mostra conclusiva Da cosa nasce cosa, a cura di Camilla Mozzato .", "links": [{"text": "Da cosa nasce cosa, a cura di Camilla Mozzato", "url": "https://www.comune.venezia.it/content/cosa-nasce-cosa-0"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/01_Da-cosa-nasce-cosa_Bevilacqua-La-Masa-San-Marco-Venezia_foto-Nico-Covre-1024x683.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Da cosa nasce cosa, Bevilacqua La Masa, San Marco, Venezia foto Nico Covre", "credit": "Exibart"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Dispiegata tra le Gallerie di Piazza San Marco e Palazzetto Tito, per poi a pprodare alla Casermetta 9 di Forte Marghera (a partire dal 3 dicembre 2026 fino al 9 maggio 2027), la mostra restituisce l’esito di quasi un anno di ricerca reciproca e co-abitativa: sono ventotto, tra artisti e collettivi della scena under 30, le diverse personalità che hanno operato negli undici mesi di residenza, in un processo vivo e dinamico in cui le pratiche, nel loro farsi, hanno abitato lo spazio dell’atelier e, insieme, si sono abitate a vicenda.", "links": [{"text": "pprodare alla Casermetta 9 di Forte Marghera", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/arte-contemporanea/tra-venezia-e-mestre-nasce-un-nuovo-spazio-per-il-contemporaneo/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "La Fondazione Bevilacqua La Masa milita sin dal 1898 a favore delle nuove generazioni artistiche, come testimonia l’esperienza novecentesca di Ca’ Pesaro, per anni spazio espositivo e fucina della scena contemporanea veneziana. Questa vocazione storica rivive, oggi, grazie alla collaborazione con Fondazione Musei Civici di Venezia, nel programma di residenza che offre agli artisti spazi di lavoro e sperimentazione, a sostegno dello sviluppo delle loro ricerche e del sorgere di una nuova geografia artistica in città."}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/12_Da-cosa-nasce-cosa_Bevilacqua-La-Masa-San-Marco-Venezia_foto-Nico-Covre-1024x683.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Da cosa nasce cosa, Bevilacqua La Masa, San Marco, Venezia foto Nico Covre", "credit": "Exibart"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.exibart.com/repository/media/2026/10/27_Da-cosa-nasce-cosa_Bevilacqua-La-Masa-San-Marco-Venezia_foto-Nico-Covre-1024x768.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Da cosa nasce cosa, Bevilacqua La Masa, San Marco, Venezia foto Nico Covre", "credit": "Exibart"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ciò che emerge nei mesi in atelier, non è tanto l’opera in quanto autonoma e compiuta, ma l’opera nel suo farsi, nel suo essere processo, nel suo stratificare le relazioni che l’hanno permeata e le interferenze che l’hanno attraversata. È proprio l’idea che da cosa nasce cosa . Il titolo riprende Da cosa nasce cosa (1981) di Bruno Munari, dove, nel solco del pensiero di Lao Tse, prende corpo l’intuizione che ogni forma sia il frutto di ciò che l’ha preceduta: errori, processi e incontri che dialogano e si concatenano l’un con l’altro. Per Munari «Da un’idea nasce un’immagine. Da un errore, spesso una scoperta. Da un incontro una direzione inattesa.»"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Allo stesso modo, le pratiche dei ventotto artisti hanno abitato l’imprevisto e la provvisorietà, procedendo per traiettorie sommerse e parallele. La mostra si propone di mapparle attraverso una cartografia situazionista e intuitiva: un tracciato che devia di continuo, che rinuncia a fissare ciò che incontra per seguirne le derive, e che restituisce lo spazio espositivo non come un territorio definito ma come un campo di relazioni sempre in via di riassestamento. Il risultato è la mappatura di una nuova scena artistica contemporanea, colta nel suo stesso processo di formazione. Nello spazio liquido della mostra, le opere crescono spontanee, sembrano ibridarsi tra loro e si disseminano di sala in sala: attraverso rimandi continui, nessun lavoro resta chiuso in sé, ma si apre alla dimensione dell’altro. article_text:
Daniel Buren nel 1971, in The Function of the Studio scrive: «Lo studio è la prima cornice, il primo limite da cui dipenderanno tutte le cornici e i limiti successivi». Buren individua nell’atelier quella sovrastruttura che predetermina ogni esposizione: uno spazio chiuso e ideologico, da lui definito “torre d’avorio” in cui l’opera si costituisce come oggetto autonomo prima di essere consegnata allo spazio espositivo. La sua pratica artistica, orientata verso una critica istituzionale, si ribella alla chiusura ideologica dell’atelier, esplicitandosi in esperienze radicali in situ , indissociabili dal contesto che le ospita e dalle relazioni che le contornano. Il paradigma bureniano presuppone tuttavia ancora un dentro e un fuori, un recinto da denunciare. Ma cosa rimane di questa opposizione quando è l’atelier stesso a divenire uno spazio poroso e permeabile, un luogo interstiziale tra l’interno e l’esterno, in cui all’autonomia dell’opera si sostituisce il processo, la relazione, la provvisorietà dello scambio, l’incontro? È l’abbattimento della torre d’avorio: su di essa nasce, ora, un terreno germinativo che sostituisce al certo, il possibile e all’autonomo, il collettivo. È entro questo orizzonte di uno studio aperto e unbound , che si può leggere l’esperienza degli Atelier 2025-2026 della Fondazione Bevilacqua La Masa di Venezia, restituita nella mostra conclusiva Da cosa nasce cosa, a cura di Camilla Mozzato .

Dispiegata tra le Gallerie di Piazza San Marco e Palazzetto Tito, per poi a pprodare alla Casermetta 9 di Forte Marghera (a partire dal 3 dicembre 2026 fino al 9 maggio 2027), la mostra restituisce l’esito di quasi un anno di ricerca reciproca e co-abitativa: sono ventotto, tra artisti e collettivi della scena under 30, le diverse personalità che hanno operato negli undici mesi di residenza, in un processo vivo e dinamico in cui le pratiche, nel loro farsi, hanno abitato lo spazio dell’atelier e, insieme, si sono abitate a vicenda.

La Fondazione Bevilacqua La Masa milita sin dal 1898 a favore delle nuove generazioni artistiche, come testimonia l’esperienza novecentesca di Ca’ Pesaro, per anni spazio espositivo e fucina della scena contemporanea veneziana. Questa vocazione storica rivive, oggi, grazie alla collaborazione con Fondazione Musei Civici di Venezia, nel programma di residenza che offre agli artisti spazi di lavoro e sperimentazione, a sostegno dello sviluppo delle loro ricerche e del sorgere di una nuova geografia artistica in città.

Ciò che emerge nei mesi in atelier, non è tanto l’opera in quanto autonoma e compiuta, ma l’opera nel suo farsi, nel suo essere processo, nel suo stratificare le relazioni che l’hanno permeata e le interferenze che l’hanno attraversata. È proprio l’idea che da cosa nasce cosa . Il titolo riprende Da cosa nasce cosa (1981) di Bruno Munari, dove, nel solco del pensiero di Lao Tse, prende corpo l’intuizione che ogni forma sia il frutto di ciò che l’ha preceduta: errori, processi e incontri che dialogano e si concatenano l’un con l’altro. Per Munari «Da un’idea nasce un’immagine. Da un errore, spesso una scoperta. Da un incontro una direzione inattesa.»

Allo stesso modo, le pratiche dei ventotto artisti hanno abitato l’imprevisto e la provvisorietà, procedendo per traiettorie sommerse e parallele. La mostra si propone di mapparle attraverso una cartografia situazionista e intuitiva: un tracciato che devia di continuo, che rinuncia a fissare ciò che incontra per seguirne le derive, e che restituisce lo spazio espositivo non come un territorio definito ma come un campo di relazioni sempre in via di riassestamento. Il risultato è la mappatura di una nuova scena artistica contemporanea, colta nel suo stesso processo di formazione. Nello spazio liquido della mostra, le opere crescono spontanee, sembrano ibridarsi tra loro e si disseminano di sala in sala: attraverso rimandi continui, nessun lavoro resta chiuso in sé, ma si apre alla dimensione dell’altro. Da cosa nasce cosa diventa un “meta-atelier” che espone sé stesso e le relazioni che su di esso si sono stratificate.

Camilla Mozzato traduce questa dimensione in presa diretta. Sceglie di dar voce agli artisti attraverso dichiarazioni e interviste che accompagnano la descrizione delle opere: le testimonianze si affiancano al percorso espositivo e restituiscono la dimensione situata e polivocale dello studio d’artista. La voce dei singoli artisti si intrecciano alle opere e agli ambienti, trasformando la mostra in una forma di etnografia diretta, capace di restituire dall’interno la vitalità e la complessità una scena nascente. Una scena che sempre più urgentemente cerca di aprire una zona temporaneamente autonoma all’interno delle logiche sistemiche e gentrificate della città. Lo fa attraverso l’autenticità dell’esperienza, l’imprevisto, la collaborazione, il radicamento, la trasversalità. Quelle stesse possibilità che, in fin dei conti, tengono in vita le pietre di Venezia.

article_text:
The Hot Springs Documentary Film Festival in Arkansas has wrapped its 35 th edition with the presentation of awards.

HSDFF ’s Critics Prize went to NAZA , the investigative documentary directed by Oscar winners Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor ( No Other Land ). The film, based on interviews with 24 anonymous members of Israeli military intelligence and soldiers, accuses Israel of callous disregard for Palestinian civilian life in its war in Gaza. Since the October 7 Hamas terror attack on Israel, the country has killed 75,000 Palestinians in the occupied territory – more than 80 percent of them civilians — according to the Gaza Ministry of Health. (The Israel Defense Forces has rejected the film’s claims, including the assertion that the IDF used artificial intelligence to determine human targets in Gaza).

Related Stories

Doc Talk Podcast Hits Road For Hot Springs Doc Festival And Conversation With Executive Director Ken Jacobson, And A Side Trip To 'Natchez'

Jurors Omaya Jones, Alissa Simon, and Al Topich praised NAZA for “using skillful and subtle editing to detail the story of the ongoing genocide in Gaza as told by the soldiers tasked with carrying it out.”

Watch on Deadline

The critics jury awarded a Special Mention to another film focused on Palestine – Edward Said: Between Worlds . Director Maiken Baird’s film examines the titular Palestinian scholar and activist who became a leading advocate for the Palestinian cause in the West. The jury lauded the film “for its expert use of archival footage and interviews to illuminate a subject who did so much to tell the story of Palestinian people.”

Once Upon a Time in Harlem , directed by David Greaves and produced by Liani Greaves and Anne de Mare, earned the festival’s award for Best Documentary Film. The film was completed from footage shot in 1972 by William Greaves (David’s father and Liani’s grandfather) that documented an unprecedented reunion of surviving members of the Harlem Renaissance.

Jurors Amanda Arya, André Robert Lee, and John Rash wrote Once Upon a Time in Harlem “is a remarkable cinematic time capsule that preserves the voices, brilliance, and cultural legacy of the Harlem Renaissance through the people who lived it. Its extraordinary archival footage and intimate storytelling make it more than a documentary.”

Jurors in that category awarded a Special Mention to American Doctor , directed by Poh Si Teng. The film centers on three American physicians – one Jewish, one Muslim, and one Zoroastrian – who volunteered their expertise in Gaza to treat Palestinian children severely wounded by Israeli armaments. “From the outset this film raises questions of ethics, political bureaucracy, and the absurdity of war,” the jurors wrote. “The filmmakers demonstrate their tremendous access and construction of story to create a poignant and important documentary that leaves audiences activated to push for change.”

Jane Elliot Against the World took the Hot Springs Matt DeCample Audience Choice Award for Best Feature. Judd Ehrlich’s film documents the extraordinary and uncompromising Iowa educator who created a “Blue Eyes/Brown Eyes exercise” to elucidate how racism functions.

The 35 th Hot Springs Documentary Film Festival honored filmmaker Joe Berlinger with the HSDFF Brent Renaud Career Achievement Award. Berlinger, an Academy Award nominee and multiple Emmy winner is known for Brother’s Keeper , the Paradise Lost Trilogy , Metallica: Some Kind of Monster , Crude: The Real Price of Oil and other films. Filmmaker Yoruba Richen, founder of Promised Land Film, was honored with HSDFF’s Impact Award.

Richen’s latest film, Free Joan Little , won the festival’s award for Best Documentary Short Film. The jury, comprised of Christopher Everett, Susan Margolin, Christine O’Malley, wrote Richen’s film “weaves rich archival material and evocative voiceover into a deeply immersive film that returns us to a landmark 1975 case, in which a young Black woman stood trial for defending herself against sexual assault by her jailer. Both gripping and historically vital, the film struck us with how urgently its questions about justice, race, and bodily autonomy still resonate today. It is a work that will spark much-needed conversation for years to come.”

A special jury mention in the shorts category went to Caitlin Ochs and Nicholas Weissman’s Black Soil . In its statement, the jury noted, “[W]e were moved by the majestic cinematography and intimate diaristic storytelling. In a world of fast paced editing, Black Soil encourages the viewer to be patient yet is engaging from beginning to end.”

Recognizing its prime position in awards season, the festival under the leadership of Hot Springs Documentary Film Institute Executive Director Ken Jacobson convened a round table in partnership with Deadline, featuring makers of four films in Oscar contention: Poh Si Teng of American Doctor ; Michał Marczak of Closure ; Biljana Tutorov of To Hold a Mountain , and Liani Greaves of Once Upon a Time in Harlem . Deadline’s Doc Talk podcast will air that round table as its new episode this Tuesday.

HSDFF ran October 9 to 17 in the historic enclave in the Ouachita Mountains. “This year’s festival, once again presented by Oaklawn, marked our 35th edition — and what a breakout year it was!” executive director Ken Jacobson commented. “From the debut of the Deadline/HSDFF Documentary Roundtable, which put the festival — and four exceptional films — front-and-center during this early peak in the Awards season — to our new Filmmaker Retreat, supporting six Mid-Southern/Southern filmmakers, HSDFF has continued to evolve in new and exciting ways. Through the outstanding collective efforts of our programming team, staff, volunteers, and Board, we have laid claim to being the region’s premiere showcase of documentary films and filmmaker-focused programs. The overwhelmingly positive response by our audiences speaks volumes about how vibrant, compelling, and essential to the fabric of our democracy the art of documentary continues to be. The story of documentary lives on!”

The 2026 Hot Springs Documentary Film Festival Award Winners:

FEATURE FILMS

HSDFF Critics Prize

NAZA

Directors: Yuval Abraham, Rachel Szor

Special Mention

EDWARD SAID: BETWEEN WORLDS

Director: Maiken Baird

Best Documentary Feature Film

ONCE UPON A TIME IN HARLEM

Director: David Greaves

Special Mention

AMERICAN DOCTOR

Director: Poh Si Teng

SHORT FILMS

Best Short Documentary Film

FREE JOAN LITTLE

Director: Yoruba Richen

Special Jury Mention

BLACK SOIL

Directors: Caitlin Ochs, Nicholas Weissman

REEL SOUTH AWARD

THE FLOOR REMEMBERS

Director: Jayme Kaye Gershen

MATT DECAMPLE AUDIENCE CHOICE AWARDS

Audience Choice Award for Best Feature

JANE ELLIOT AGAINST THE WORLD

Director: Judd Ehrlich

Runner Up

DARLENE LOVE: I KNOW WHERE I’VE BEEN

Director: Barry Avrich

Audience Choice Award for Best Short

TAMPONS & TAXES: OR HOW TO PLAY THE OLE BOYS’ CLUB AND WIN

Director: Emily Harrold

Runner Up

THE BADDEST SPEECHWRITER OF ALL

Director: Ben Proudfoot

article_text:
He was six years old. He was handed a Bolex 8mm camera, complete with its full editing kit, the way other children are given a ball or a bicycle. “I was immediately fascinated by moving images, and by the manipulation of those images through editing,” Cheyco Leidmann recalls. He cites Orson Welles and Touch of Evil , a film that “branded him.” Listening to him, it becomes clear that everything starts there: in the early conviction that an image never really tells the truth.

Cheyco Leidmann has never presented himself as a photographer. “These aren’t photos,” he was already correcting people in 1998. “Anyone can be a photographer these days, even with a phone. No, these are images. They’re worked.” It has to be understood this way: no Photoshop, no editing, everything shot on slide film, everything done in the camera. A red, ketchup-colored ice cream, a California license plate reading “FOXY LADY,” a green latex-gloved hand gripping a Cadillac hood. For him, genuine artistic value is the product of meticulous, almost surgical work, the point where glamour, provocation and art collide.

There is something of Nadar in this way of building a myth before the work itself, something of Kerouac in the American road he never stopped traveling, Downtown LA, Soda Lake, Fort Lauderdale, and a touch of Buñuel in these bodies that emerge from cars like surrealist apparitions. He himself prefers to cite Hunter S. Thompson. “One of my favorite books is Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas ,” he confides. Reading him, it is no longer surprising that his world resembles a hallucinated road trip in which advertising has seized power.

Foxy Lady was published right in the fertile years of the 1980s and became an instant cult object, sold out, reissued, copied to the point of exhaustion. “My style got copied, admired, criticized and, worse still, my images were stolen,” he said of his 2018 collaboration with stylist Adam Selman. “These are individuals who use other people’s ideas because they are too poor to create something of their own.” The line lands hard.

His longtime creative partner is Ypsitylla von Nazareth, stylist and muse, present since Foxy Lady through his most recent campaigns. “She has taken charge of every production process that followed, right up to today,” he says of her, with the same economy of words he reserves for what truly matters.

From California light, Leidmann shifted one day toward darker visions, the series Toxytt, its fragments, its frontal violence. The shift is surprising, given how opposed the two worlds seem, yet he speaks of it with the same quiet nonchalance. Asked about any regrets, he first deflects, “I am completely low tech,” before delivering the line that sums up his entire system: “I do not try to find out what technique you use to eat.” People inevitably read provocation into it. He defends himself with the same economy of words: “Provoking for the sake of provoking is like buying a ticket to your own concert: it is pointless. It is simply what I feel.”

Then there is the question of the gesture itself, of what happens in the instant of the shutter click. On the secret of the perfect frame: “The eyes are the weapon. You have to think subversively. It all comes down to speed, experience, discipline, reaction, precision and luck, all coming together in a moment of nihilistic silence,” he told Dazed . A few words later, he adds that under these conditions, nine shots out of ten come out right. He is to be believed.

Art? He calls the word “unpleasant, inflationary, a sticker, a price tag, a tool of manipulation.” Cheyco Leidmann thinks as he pleases, lives as he pleases, wherever he pleases, Paris, New York, Miami, Los Angeles, never settling anywhere. “I consider myself a restless, cosmopolitan man,” he says, “I live where I like to live, in Toxytt City,” a city of his own invention, entirely fabricated yet entirely believable, much like his photographs. At YellowKorner, the series “Foxy Lady” and “Silicon” hold the two ends of this America: chrome-plated California on one side, humid Florida on the other. The colors have not shifted a shade.
