editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "July Jung、金度延和宋诗曦谈《Dora》", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "一部受弗洛伊德的朵拉启发、历时二十年打磨的电影", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "July Jung带着她的第三部长片《Dora》重返釜山，此前她的作品有《道熙呀》（2014）和《下一个素熙》（2022）。这三部作品均在戛纳电影节首映，《Dora》在五月的导演双周单元进行世界首映后，又亮相釜山国际电影节的“大师放映”单元。影片受弗洛伊德对朵拉的病例研究启发，讲述了一名患有神秘疾病的十八岁女孩经历充满巨变的一个夏天的故事。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "与July Jung一同出席的有主演金度延——她曾是 Weki Meki 成员，凭借金敏荷的《Idiot Girls and School Ghost: School Anniversary》获得青龙电影奖最佳新人女演员奖——以及在继《道熙呀》十二年后再次与导演合作的宋诗曦。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "他们讨论了导演在二十多岁时首次萌生的一个想法、漫长的创作历程以及邀请日本女演员安藤樱饰演娜美（Nami）的过程。", "translated": true}, {"type": "heading", "text": "《Dora》正在釜山国际电影节放映", "links": [{"text": "Busan International Film Festival", "url": "https://www.biff.kr/eng/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://asianmoviepulse.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Busan-2026.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Asian Movie Pulse", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你的电影片名都是角色的名字，从《道熙呀》（《A Girl at My Door》）到《下一个素熙》，再到如今的《Dora》，它们都是拥有强大女性角色的电影。《Dora》是如何开始的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "正如你所说，这很可能就是这些以主角命名的电影的起点。在我二十多岁的时候，我偶然读到了弗洛伊德关于朵拉及其歇斯底里的病例研究，我对此着迷不已。当时我想，如果我以后拍电影，我很想以这个故事为蓝本拍一部。当我第一次尝试写剧本时，脑子里浮现的就是这个故事。但我以前从未写过剧本，结果并不顺利。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我把它记在心底，先拍了《道熙呀》。那部拍完后，这个故事又回到了我脑海中，我便开始潜心创作剧本。我完成了第一稿并尝试让这部电影投拍，但未能成行。读过剧本的人说看不懂在讲什么，尤其是投资人觉得太难了。我坚持了很久，最后还是放弃了。在那之后，我拍了《下一个素熙》，直到那时我才回到最初的起点，拍了《Dora》。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "所以这可能是你经过漫长等待才拍出的电影。如果观众想要欣赏它，或者从不同的角度看待它，应该注意什么？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当这个故事最初找到我时，我大约是朵拉那个年纪。时光流逝，等我拍这部电影时，我感觉自己与娜美的距离近了许多。因此，现在我内心并存着两样东西：那时的年轻的我和如今身为年长一代成年人的我。如果观众好奇我为什么要拍这部电影，我希望他们在观看时能记这一点。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "金度延，你把朵拉演绎得极为出色。在扮演她时，你找到了什么乐趣？这个过程最让你有成就感的是什么？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当我第一次读剧本时，我觉得我和朵拉非常不同。我很纳闷自己该如何去理解她，因为她的选择与我的选择大相径庭，起初我觉得她非常遥远。但随着与导演不断地交流，我渐渐走近了她。在读剧本时，我甚至给导演发了一条短信，说每读一遍，每一句台词都变得更加美丽，层层递进。所以，理解这个故事的过程对我来说是快乐而感动的，拍摄本身也是一种乐趣。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "那是一个紧张而艰难的夏天，每个人都付出了努力。但这是我从未做过的一种工作。我们有日本演员加入，摄影师和摄影团队来自法国。这一切都是崭新而有趣的，我学到了很多东西。能够如此深地沉浸在一个角色中，对我来说是一段宝贵的经历。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "宋诗曦，看过《道熙呀》的人都会记住你，你再次回到了导演的世界，或许已成为其中的核心人物之一。你饰演的延秀成为了片中事件的催化剂。再次与她合作感觉如何？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "昨天导演给我发了几张照片。那是我们十二年前拍的电影《道熙呀》的剧照。自己说可能有点不好意思，但我们俩当时看起来都挺可爱的。我想，难道真的已经过去十二年了吗？时间过得真快。如今时隔十二年在合作，我个人在片场最大的感受是：导演一点也没变——她在塑造每个角色时的导演手法依然细腻，她的世界依然深邃。她会把很多东西悬置很久，然后在决定的时刻指明方向。她这种创作方式的自由度对我极具吸引力，也帮助我更贴近我的角色。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你片中的年轻女性角色常常发现自己身处一个由成年人组成的世界中，这些成年人对她们的感受不屑一顾，无法倾听或理解她们。你能详细谈谈你刻意呈现这种动态的初衷吗？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "是的，朵拉显然一直在经历种种不适。朵拉出发时的那个世界包括她的父母和她父亲的朋友，成年人在那里消磨时间，但也有他们的孩子（包括双龄胎）以及她同龄的朋友。由于与她交流情感、建立关系、互相影响的人都是成年人，这看起来可能是一个成年人的世界。但我并不认为她的青春期是她产生痛苦根源的原因。她只是那种处境中最脆弱的存在而已。不过，周围的人最初在修复她脆弱、生病的状态方面发挥了巨大的推动作用。随后她逐渐康复，达到了能够完全独自站立的地步，而就在那时，情况急转直下。人们可能会纳闷，他们其实是不是并不希望她康复？我认为由此产生的困惑主导了影片的后半部分。我最想探讨的是朵拉在这种困惑中如何行事、她做出了什么选择，以及她如何走向结局。暂无更多，以上即全部内容……（注：根据切片对应原文，此处若被拆分，保持直译即可）", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "起初，她身边的人在恢复她那脆弱、病弱的状态方面发挥了巨大的推动作用。随后，她逐渐康复，达到了可以完全独立站立的地步，而正是在那个时候，局势突然发生了变化。人们可能会疑惑，他们是否其实并不希望她康复，我认为由此产生的困惑主导了影片的后半部分。我最想探讨的是，朵拉在这种困惑中如何行动、她作出了什么选择，以及她是如何走向结局的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你之前提到你是在二十多岁时首次创作剧本的。那部最初的剧本和成片相似吗？你对结局有什么看法？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "最初，弗洛伊德的记述中吸引我的是围绕着这个女孩的人际关系与心理力量。但多年后，当我为了将其拍成电影而再次审视它时，我突然意识到，这一切全都是那个男人所看到的东西，这让我感到震惊。我几乎被它压垮了。我问自己：朵拉的声音在哪里？它真的抓住了她想要的东西吗？难道我们从来都只是通过他来审视她吗？从那时起，我认为这部电影应该超越那种记述，我便琢磨，如果完全从朵拉自己的声音出发来讲述这个故事会怎样。这与弗洛伊德最初的报告有着巨大差异，这也成为了这部电影的驱动力。在他的案例中，她从未康复，故事以她生病且未接受治疗而告终。我一直在思考，它如何能变成另一种类型的案例——一个她靠自己康复并完整站起来的案例。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "结局其实我在初稿里就已经写好了。但通往这个结局的步骤并不充分，所以创作工作屡屡受阻，有些部分始终无法契合。最终，完成的剧本与初稿并没有太大区别。主要的发展是一样的，但紧密交织的人物关系和他们的行动一点一点地发生了改变，我正是通过这种方式才得以呈现现在的结局。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "朵拉展现了非常微妙的情感。金多妍，你是如何为这个角色做准备的？与其他演员之间的默契又如何？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这种默契是在我们逐渐互相了解的过程中建立起来的，我很珍视演员们共同构建的这一过程。对我来说最重要、也是最困难但必不可通过的过程，某种程度上和我在一开始所说的一样。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我记得那大概是在我的第一轮试镜时。我当时只拿到了片段，觉得非常难。那是与医生的一场戏，对手戏演员是一位资深演员。在不知道其他剧情的情况下，我只读了那部分，然后我问导演，朵拉那一刻是不是在说谎。她告诉我，朵拉一直在说真话。那一刻我想，当所有人都把真话当成谎言时，她独自坚守真实该有多孤独、多艰难啊。我在为这个角色试镜，连我都曾怀疑过她。在准备期间，初次试镜的画面一次又一次地浮现在我脑海中。我需要不断地切换视角，以第三方和朵拉的身份去体会，直到我能真正走入她的内心。这是我所需要的过程，我也为此付出了很多努力。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "安藤樱的选角是怎么促成的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "从初稿开始确实有一点改变，就是这个：这个角色原本是个韩国人。我从未想过跟外国演员合作，也从未真正考虑过其他国家的人。然后，在某个时刻，我突然开始怀疑：我是否真的能完全理解那种空虚与孤独的深度？即便我拍了这部电影，亲自写了剧本并出演这个角色，也依然会有我不知道的部分。这种认知对我的触动很大。与此同时，我又在想：如果她不是韩国人，而是日本人呢？几乎在同一瞬间，我想到了：那就找安藤樱吧。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "那就是我那天闪过的念头。但我对安藤樱的了解仅限于作为观众。我没有任何私人联系方式，也没有办法联系她，所以当时只是自己一个人在脑海里琢磨。后来，我决定试一试。我通过她的经纪公司联系了她，询问她是否有兴趣出演一部韩国电影。她说她想了解更多并看看剧本。我让人把剧本翻译成日文，大约一个月后发了过去。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "为什么是日本人，又为什么是安藤樱？这或许是因为我是日本电影的超级崇拜者。当我观看她在众多电影中的表演时，我感到十分惊叹：每一个角色都是一个完全不同的人，然而又有一种感觉——这依然是安藤樱。我想，在娜美那些我尚未知晓或无法知晓的部分里，像她这样的演员或许能让一个名为“娜美”的人在我与演员之间真实存在，并且我们能够共同塑造这个角色。我反复思量，然后伸出了橄榄枝。幸运的是，她读了剧本并表示想见一面，于是我们就见面了。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "起初，她对韩语台词感到非常苦恼；她以前从未说过韩语。尽管如此，她还是希望能让这部电影、娜美这个角色以及娜美与朵拉的故事焕发生机，我们也就是这样走到了一起。我真的非常幸运。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这部电影被评为仅限成年人观看，其中包含了亲密戏份，这对于你来说还是第一次。金多妍，你在接演这个角色之前有什么顾虑吗？拍完这些戏后你有什么感受？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "说实话，我起初几乎没有产生过这种顾虑。尽管这是我第一次拍摄亲密戏，但在读剧本时我自然而然地接受了，所以并没有为此困扰。在这个过程中，导演和我更详细地探讨了我们要如何拍摄，她多次询问我是否感到自在，并认真倾听了我的想法。她越是这样，我便越努力去理解剧本：这个场面是如何编写的，为什么它是必要的。我询问了导演，进而认识到这个场面在我们电影中非常重要。娜美（Nami）和多拉（Dora）各自带着自己的伤痛，而她们第一次向彼此全然敞开并借此建立连接，这对于电影来说是不可或缺的。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "作为演员我必须去拍摄它，而作为一个普通人，这对我而言也不可能毫无波澜，因此我很好奇它将会如何呈现，而导演对此有着非常坚定的想法。因为她对女性的身体、以及随之而来的情感有着如此深刻的理解，我渐渐确信自己无需担忧，这种信任让我能够全身心地投入到角色中。在片场，我的搭档给了我极大的帮助并随时确认我的状态，我非常依赖她。工作人员也非常体贴。我们还配备了一位亲密行为协调员（intimacy coordinator）。这是我第一次与亲密行为协调员合作，我开始觉得这真的是必不可少的。多亏了这些，我才能安心地完成拍摄。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "郑朱莉在发布会尾声时表示，她希望这部电影能打动观看它的观众，并引发丰富多样的反应与意见。", "translated": true}]
article_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "July Jung, Kim Do-yeon and Song Sae-byeok on “Dora”"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "A film inspired by Freud’s Dora, two decades in the making"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "July Jung returns to Busan with “Dora”, her third feature after “A Girl at My Door” (2014) and “Next Sohee” (2022). All three have premiered at Cannes, and “Dora” arrives at the Busan International Film Festival, in the Gala Presentation section, after its world premiere in the Directors’ Fortnight in May. Inspired by Freud’s case study of Dora, the film follows an eighteen-year-old girl suffering from a mysterious illness who experiences a summer full of changes."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "July Jung was joined by lead actress Kim Do-yeon, a former Weki Meki member who won Best New Actress at the Blue Dragon Film Awards for Kim Min-ha’s “Idiot Girls and School Ghost: School Anniversary”, and by Song Sae-byeok, who reunited with her for this new film, twelve years after “A Girl at My Door”."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "They discussed an idea the director first had in her twenties, the long road to making it and the casting of Japanese actress Sakura Ando as Nami."}, {"type": "heading", "text": "Dora is screening at Busan International Film Festival", "links": [{"text": "Busan International Film Festival", "url": "https://www.biff.kr/eng/"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://asianmoviepulse.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Busan-2026.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "Asian Movie Pulse"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The titles of your films are the names of their characters, from Dohee-ya (“A Girl at My Door”) to “Next Sohee” and now “Dora”, and they are all films with powerful female characters. How did Dora start?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "As you say, it may well be the starting point for the films that carry their protagonists’ names. In my twenties I came across Freud’s case study of Dora and her hysteria, and I was fascinated by it. I thought that if I ever made films, I would like to make one from this story. When I first tried to write a screenplay, this was the story that came to mind. But I had never written a screenplay before, and it didn’t work."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I kept it in the back of my mind and made “A Girl at My Door” first. When that was finished, the story came back to me, and I worked hard on a screenplay. I completed a first draft and tried to get the film produced, but it didn’t happen. People who read it said they couldn’t tell what was going on, and the investors in particular said it was too difficult. I pushed for a long time and then abandoned it. After that I made “Next Sohee”, and only then did I go back to where I had started and made “Dora”."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "So this may be a film you made after a long wait. What should the audience pay attention to if they want to enjoy it, or see it differently?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "When this story first came to me, I was around Dora’s age. Time has passed, and by the time I was making the film I felt I had grown much closer to Nami. So two things now coexist in me: the young person I was then and the adult of an older generation I am today. If viewers wonder why I made this film, I hope they will keep that in mind as they watch."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Kim Do-yeon, you portrayed Dora wonderfully. What joy did you find in playing her, and what was most rewarding about the process?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "When I first read the script, I thought Dora and I were very different. I wondered how I was supposed to understand her, because her choices were so unlike what I would have chosen, and at first she felt very far away. But as I kept talking with the director, I gradually grew closer to her. While reading the script I even sent the director a text message saying that every sentence grew more beautiful the more I read, layer by layer. So the process of understanding this story was happy and moving for me, and shooting was a joy as well."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It was an intense and difficult summer, and everyone worked hard. But it was a kind of work I had never done before. We had a Japanese actor with us, and the cinematographer and camera team came from France. All of it was new and fun, and I learned a great deal. Being able to immerse myself so deeply in a role was a precious experience for me."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Song Sae-byeok, those who saw “A Girl at My Door” will remember you, and you have come back to the director’s world, perhaps as one of its essential figures. You play Yeon-su, who becomes a catalyst for events in the film. What was it like to work with her again?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Yesterday the director sent me a few photos. They were stills from “A Girl at My Door”, a film we made twelve years ago. It’s awkward to say it myself, but we both looked rather cute. I thought, has it really been twelve years? Time passes. Now that we have worked together again after twelve years, what I felt on set, personally, was that the director is just the same as ever: the delicacy of her direction in shaping each character, and the depth of her world. She leaves things open for a long time, and then at the decisive moment she points the way. That freedom in her approach is very attractive to me, and it helped me get closer to my character."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Your young female characters often find themselves in a world of adults who dismiss their feelings and are unable to listen to them or understand them. Could you elaborate on your intention in portraying this dynamic?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Yes, Dora clearly keeps experiencing discomfort. The world Dora sets out from includes her parents and friends of her father, and the adults spend time together there, but there are also their children, including twins, and friends of her own age. It may look like a world of adults because the people with whom she exchanges emotions, forms relationships, and influences and is influenced are adults. But I don’t think her youth is what creates the root of her discomfort. She is simply the most vulnerable being in that situation."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "At first the people around her are a great driving force in restoring her fragile, ill state. Then she gradually recovers and reaches the point where she can stand entirely on her own, and at that point things change abruptly. One may wonder whether they did not actually want her to recover, and I think the confusion that arises from there dominates the second half of the film. What I most wanted to explore was how Dora acts in that confusion, what choices she makes, and how she heads toward the end."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "You said earlier that you first worked on a screenplay in your twenties. Is that first screenplay similar to the finished film? And what were your thoughts about the ending?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "At the beginning, what interested me in Freud’s account was the relationships and psychological forces that surround the girl. article_text:
July Jung, Kim Do-yeon and Song Sae-byeok on “Dora”

A film inspired by Freud’s Dora, two decades in the making

July Jung returns to Busan with “Dora”, her third feature after “A Girl at My Door” (2014) and “Next Sohee” (2022). All three have premiered at Cannes, and “Dora” arrives at the Busan International Film Festival, in the Gala Presentation section, after its world premiere in the Directors’ Fortnight in May. Inspired by Freud’s case study of Dora, the film follows an eighteen-year-old girl suffering from a mysterious illness who experiences a summer full of changes.

July Jung was joined by lead actress Kim Do-yeon, a former Weki Meki member who won Best New Actress at the Blue Dragon Film Awards for Kim Min-ha’s “Idiot Girls and School Ghost: School Anniversary”, and by Song Sae-byeok, who reunited with her for this new film, twelve years after “A Girl at My Door”.

They discussed an idea the director first had in her twenties, the long road to making it and the casting of Japanese actress Sakura Ando as Nami.

Dora is screening at Busan International Film Festival

The titles of your films are the names of their characters, from Dohee-ya (“A Girl at My Door”) to “Next Sohee” and now “Dora”, and they are all films with powerful female characters. How did Dora start?

As you say, it may well be the starting point for the films that carry their protagonists’ names. In my twenties I came across Freud’s case study of Dora and her hysteria, and I was fascinated by it. I thought that if I ever made films, I would like to make one from this story. When I first tried to write a screenplay, this was the story that came to mind. But I had never written a screenplay before, and it didn’t work.

I kept it in the back of my mind and made “A Girl at My Door” first. When that was finished, the story came back to me, and I worked hard on a screenplay. I completed a first draft and tried to get the film produced, but it didn’t happen. People who read it said they couldn’t tell what was going on, and the investors in particular said it was too difficult. I pushed for a long time and then abandoned it. After that I made “Next Sohee”, and only then did I go back to where I had started and made “Dora”.

So this may be a film you made after a long wait. What should the audience pay attention to if they want to enjoy it, or see it differently?

When this story first came to me, I was around Dora’s age. Time has passed, and by the time I was making the film I felt I had grown much closer to Nami. So two things now coexist in me: the young person I was then and the adult of an older generation I am today. If viewers wonder why I made this film, I hope they will keep that in mind as they watch.

Kim Do-yeon, you portrayed Dora wonderfully. What joy did you find in playing her, and what was most rewarding about the process?

When I first read the script, I thought Dora and I were very different. I wondered how I was supposed to understand her, because her choices were so unlike what I would have chosen, and at first she felt very far away. But as I kept talking with the director, I gradually grew closer to her. While reading the script I even sent the director a text message saying that every sentence grew more beautiful the more I read, layer by layer. So the process of understanding this story was happy and moving for me, and shooting was a joy as well.

It was an intense and difficult summer, and everyone worked hard. But it was a kind of work I had never done before. We had a Japanese actor with us, and the cinematographer and camera team came from France. All of it was new and fun, and I learned a great deal. Being able to immerse myself so deeply in a role was a precious experience for me.

Song Sae-byeok, those who saw “A Girl at My Door” will remember you, and you have come back to the director’s world, perhaps as one of its essential figures. You play Yeon-su, who becomes a catalyst for events in the film. What was it like to work with her again?

Yesterday the director sent me a few photos. They were stills from “A Girl at My Door”, a film we made twelve years ago. It’s awkward to say it myself, but we both looked rather cute. I thought, has it really been twelve years? Time passes. Now that we have worked together again after twelve years, what I felt on set, personally, was that the director is just the same as ever: the delicacy of her direction in shaping each character, and the depth of her world. She leaves things open for a long time, and then at the decisive moment she points the way. That freedom in her approach is very attractive to me, and it helped me get closer to my character.

Your young female characters often find themselves in a world of adults who dismiss their feelings and are unable to listen to them or understand them. Could you elaborate on your intention in portraying this dynamic?

Yes, Dora clearly keeps experiencing discomfort. The world Dora sets out from includes her parents and friends of her father, and the adults spend time together there, but there are also their children, including twins, and friends of her own age. It may look like a world of adults because the people with whom she exchanges emotions, forms relationships, and influences and is influenced are adults. But I don’t think her youth is what creates the root of her discomfort. She is simply the most vulnerable being in that situation.

At first the people around her are a great driving force in restoring her fragile, ill state. Then she gradually recovers and reaches the point where she can stand entirely on her own, and at that point things change abruptly. One may wonder whether they did not actually want her to recover, and I think the confusion that arises from there dominates the second half of the film. What I most wanted to explore was how Dora acts in that confusion, what choices she makes, and how she heads toward the end.

You said earlier that you first worked on a screenplay in your twenties. Is that first screenplay similar to the finished film? And what were your thoughts about the ending?

At the beginning, what interested me in Freud’s account was the relationships and psychological forces that surround the girl. But when I looked at it again after many years, wanting to make it into a film, it struck me that all of it was what that man had seen, and that was a shock. I felt almost overpowered by it. I asked myself: is Dora’s voice here? Does it really grasp what she wants? Haven’t we only ever seen her through him? From there I thought the film should overcome that account, and I wondered what would happen if I told the story entirely in Dora’s own voice. That is the big difference from Freud’s original report, and it became the driving force of the film. In his case, she never recovered, and it ended with her ill and untreated. I kept thinking about how it could become another kind of case, one in which she recovers by herself and stands up whole.

The ending was something I had already written in the first draft. But the steps leading to that ending were not sufficient, so the work kept stalling, and some parts never fell into place. In the end, the finished screenplay is not very different from the first draft. The major developments are the same, but the relationships between characters and their actions, woven in tightly, changed little by little, and that is how I was able to reach the ending as it is now.

Dora expresses very subtle emotions. Kim Do-yeon, how did you prepare for the role, and how was the rapport with the other actors?

It grew as we got to know one another, and I value that process, which the actors built together. The most important process for me, and the most difficult but necessary one, was in a way similar to what I said at the start.

I remember it was probably at my first audition. I had received only excerpts, and I found it very hard. It was a scene with the doctor, with a senior actor in the other role. I read only that part without knowing the rest of the story, and I asked the director whether Dora was lying at that moment. She told me that Dora keeps telling the truth. At that moment I thought how lonely and difficult it must be for her to be telling the truth while everyone treats it as a lie. I was auditioning for her role and even I doubted her. That first audition came back to me again and again while I was preparing. I needed to keep switching perspectives, as a third party and as Dora, until I could come to know her heart. It was a process I needed, and I worked hard at it.

How did the casting of Sakura Ando come about?

One thing did change from the first draft, and this is it: the character was originally Korean. I had never imagined making a film with a foreign actor, and I had never really thought of people from other countries. Then at some point I wondered whether I could ever fully understand the depth of Nami’s emptiness and loneliness. Even if I made the film, wrote it and played the part myself, there would be parts I did not know. That realization was a big one for me. At the same time I wondered: what if she were Japanese rather than Korean? And almost in the same moment, I thought: then it would be Sakura Ando.

That was my train of thought that day. But I only knew Sakura Ando as a member of the audience. I had no personal connection and no way to contact her, so I was just thinking about it by myself. Then I decided to try. I contacted her through her management and asked whether she would be interested in a film in Korea. She said she would like to hear more and see the script. I had the screenplay translated into Japanese and sent it about a month later.

Why Japanese, and why Sakura Ando? It may be because I am a great admirer of Japanese cinema. When I watch her performances across many films, I find it astonishing that every role is a completely different person, and yet there is also a sense that this is simply Sakura. I thought that in whatever part of Nami I did not yet know, or could not know, an actor like her might make it possible for a person called Nami to exist between me and the actor, and that we could build this character together. I kept thinking about it, and then I reached out. Fortunately, she read the script and said she wanted to meet, and we met.

At first she agonized a great deal over the Korean dialogue; she had never spoken Korean before. Nevertheless, she wanted to bring this film, the character of Nami, and Nami’s story with Dora to life, and that is how we came to work together. I was very lucky.

The film is rated for adults only and includes intimate scenes, a first for you. Kim Do-yeon, did you have any concerns before taking the role, and how did you feel after shooting them?

Honestly, I hardly felt such concerns at first. Even though it was my first time shooting an intimate scene, I accepted it naturally when I read the script, so I wasn’t troubled by it. In the process, the director and I talked in more detail about how we would shoot it, and she asked me many times whether I was comfortable and listened carefully to what I said. The more she did, the more I tried to understand the script: how the scene is written and why it is needed. I asked the director, and I came to see that this scene is very important in our film. Nami and Dora each carry their own wounds, and showing them fully to each other for the first time, and connecting through that, is essential to the film.

As an actor I had to shoot it, and as a person it could not be nothing to me, so I was curious how it would be expressed, and the director had very firm thoughts about it. Because she understands the female body, and therefore the feelings that go with it, so well, I came to trust that I didn’t need to worry, and that trust let me throw myself into the character. On set, my scene partner helped me a great deal and checked on how I was doing, and I relied on her. The staff were very considerate as well. We also had an intimacy coordinator. It was my first time working with one, and I came to feel it is truly necessary. Thanks to that, I was able to shoot with peace of mind.

July Jung closed the conference by saying she hopes the film will move those who watch it and draw a wide range of reactions and opinions.

editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "为 Frieze 周做好准备，伦敦各大机构迎来艺术博览会、全新展览和秋季展季的开幕", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "艺术界正紧锣密鼓地筹备将于下周在摄政公园（Regent’s Park）举办的 Frieze London 和 Frieze Masters 艺博会，展期为 14-18 October。摄影、基于镜头的媒介以及与图像相关的展示占据了重要地位。Frieze London 推出了由北京中间美术馆馆长、第19届伊斯坦布尔双年展（2027）联合策展人鲁迎华（Carol Yinghua Lu）甄选的策划单元“代码宇宙：审视后数码时代的艺术家”（The Code Universe: Artists Interrogating a Post-Digital Age）。该单元包含可追溯至 1970 年代末的作品，探讨了大众文化及其生产、传播和消费方式，其中包括跨媒介创作拼贴与雕塑作品的日本艺术家大竹伸朗（Shinro Ohtake，由 greengrassi 与 Take Ninagawa 代理）。此外，展会还带来了朱昶（Payne Zhu，Spurs Gallery）的一件全新多通道视频装置，探讨人类感知与机器认知之间的关系。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在 Frieze London 的策展单元之外，PM8 / Francisco Salas 将呈现立陶宛艺术家阿尔吉尔达斯·谢什库斯（Algirdas Šeškus）的历史彩色照片。这些照片拍摄于他在苏联时期接受的唯一一次官方委约，但当时因不符合“官方艺术”既定标准而被拒绝。Edel Assanti 将呈现由波兰艺术家马尔cin·杜德克（Marcin Dudek）根据其童年住宅设计的“记忆盒”展位，并展出温卡·彼得森（Vinca Petersen）和谢达·索莱马尼（Sheida Soleimani）等艺术家的作品。莫林·帕利画廊（Maureen Paley）的参展艺术家包括安妮·哈迪（Anne Hardy）、彼得·胡贾尔（Peter Hujar）和沃尔夫冈·蒂尔曼斯（Wolfgang Tillmans），而 Soft Opening 带来的艺术家则包括埃本·索迪波（Eben Sodipo），其作品涵盖混合媒介摄影拼贴。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Frieze Masters 推出了一条名为“将现代主义酷儿化：20 世纪的视觉语言”（Queering Modernism: Visual Languages of the 20 th Century）的观展路线，由德国策展人安克·肯普克斯（Anke Kempkes）构思，并汇集了克劳德·卡汉（Claude Cahun，由 Alberta Pane Gallery 代理）和露丝·伯恩哈德（Ruth Bernhard，Galerie Albrecht）等影像先锋。Frieze Masters 的焦点单元（Spotlight）还包括其他被西方正统忽视的艺术家，例如中国影像创作者郎静山（Each Modern）——他是 1930 和 40 年代复合摄影的先驱，将多张底片与绘画、题字和刮擦相结合。Frieze 还将重返当代艺术研究所（Institute of Contemporary Arts），带来全新的艺术家电影与动态影像作品展映，在 Frieze 周期间循环播放，并可在 ica.art 在线观看。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Reengrassi__Take_Ninagawa_Shinro_Ohtake_RetinaYellow_RAM_2_2025.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Retina/Yellow RAM 2, 2025 © Shinro Ohtake. Courtesy of the Artist, Take Ninagawa, Tokyo and greengrassi, London", "credit": "British Journal of Photography", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Luo-Bonian-Drawing-Water-from-a-Well-May-1932.-Estate-of-Luo-Bonian.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Drawing Water from a Well, May 1932 by Luo Bonian. © Estate of Luo Bonian, on show in Light and Magic: The Birth of Art Photography on show at Tate Modern", "credit": "British Journal of Photography", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在 Frieze 之外，商业画廊中还有一系列精彩展览，各大机构的全新展季也纷纷拉开帷幕。例如，摄影画廊（The Photographers’ Gallery）今年秋季将目光聚焦于色彩，展出威廉·埃格尔斯顿（William Eggleston）的经典影像以及桑莱·索里（Sanlé Sory）的彩色肖像，其中部分作品此前从未公开发表。国家肖像馆（National Portrait Gallery）也通过蒂姆·沃克（Tim Walker）的展览《仙境》（Fairyland）拥抱了一场色彩风暴，该展探讨了酷儿身份、爱与社群。泰特英国美术馆（Tate Britain）的《90年代：艺术与时尚》（The 90s: Art and Fashion）刚刚开幕；平心而论，外界对其评价褒贬不一，但它确实囊括了于尔根·特勒（Juergen Teller）、艾琳·佩里尔（Eileen Perrier）和奈杰尔·沙弗兰（Nigel Shafran）等备受赞誉的摄影项目。在泰特现代美术馆（Tate Modern），《光与魔力：艺术摄影的诞生》（Light and Magic: The Birth of Art Photography）是一场关于画意摄影（Pictorialism）的新展，强调了其国际化的传播；这场备受期待的展览有望重振人们对这一长期被忽视流派的兴趣。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Graces Mews 正在呈献《从裁切中涌现》（What Rose from the Cut），这是对热门女性主义拼贴画展《玫瑰》（The Rose）的全新演变。该展由艺术家贾斯汀·库兰德（Justine Kurland）、策展人兼收藏家萨拉·米勒·梅igs（Sarah Miller Meigs）、展场主办方，以及 V&A 博物馆摄影界女性帕拉索尔基金会策展人、新书《剪切：摄影拼贴的女性主义历史》（Cut Out: A Feminist History of Photo Collage）作者菲奥娜·罗杰斯（Fiona Rogers）共同策划。从克劳德·卡汉等历史艺术家的作品，一直深入到凯莎·斯卡维尔（Keisha Scarville）等当代的创作，该展为一种始终保持先锋姿态的形式带来了令人兴奋的全新视角。拼贴艺术也同样亮相豪瑟与沃斯画廊（Hauser and Wirth），带来洛娜·辛普森（Lorna Simpson）作品的全新展示，其中亦包含她的绘画与雕塑；这是一个双人展，同时还展出了辛迪·舍曼（Cindy Sherman）的作品，包括其全新系列《面料主妇》（Fabric Matrons）。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.1854.photography/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/PreviousOngoing_LSimpson_2026_PhotoCred_JamesWang_300dpi-hires.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "Previous & Ongoing, 2026 © Lorna Simpson. article_text:
Get ready get set for Frieze week, as London opens the art fairs, new shows and Autumn seasons in the big institutions

The art world is gearing up for Frieze London and Frieze Masters fairs next week, which are open in Regent’s Park from 14-18 October. Photography, lens-based media and image-adjacent presentations figure large, with Frieze London featuring a curated programme including The Code Universe: Artists Interrogating a Post-Digital Age , selected by Carol Yinghua Lu, director of the Inside-Out Art Museum, Beijing, and co-curator of the 19th Istanbul Biennial (2027). Including work dating back to the late 1970s, it considers popular culture and the way it is produced, circulated and consumed, and includes Japanese artist Shinro Ohtake (presented by greengrassi and Take Ninagawa), who works across media to create collages and sculptural pieces. It also includes a new multi-channel video installation by Payne Zhu (Spurs Gallery), which explores the relationship between human perception and machine cognition.

Outside the curated section at Frieze London, PM8 / Francisco Salas will present historical colour photographs by Lithuanian artist Algirdas Šeškus, which were taken on the only official commission he received during Soviet times, but rejected as they did not fit the given standards of ‘official art’. Edel Assanti will present a ‘memory box’ booth designed by Polish artist Marcin Dudek after his childhood home, and show works by artists such as Vinca Petersen and Sheida Soleimani. Maureen Paley’s presentation will include Anne Hardy, Peter Hujar and Wolfgang Tillmans, while Soft Opening’s artists will include Ebun Sodipo, whose work includes mixed-media photographic collages.

Frieze Masters includes a trail titled Queering Modernism: Visual Languages of the 20 th Century , conceived of by German curator Anke Kempkes and featuring image-pioneers such as Claude Cahun (presented by Alberta Pane Gallery) and Ruth Bernhard (Galerie Albrecht). The spotlight section at Frieze Masters includes other artists neglected by the Western canon, including Chinese image-maker Lang JingShan (Each Modern) – a pioneer of composite photography in the 1930s and 40s, who combined multiple negatives with painting, inscription, and scratching. Frieze also returns to the Institute of Contemporary Arts with a new programme of artists’ film and moving-image works, screening on a continuous loop during Frieze Week and online at ica.art.

Beyond Frieze is a host of interesting shows in commercial galleries, plus new seasons opening across the big institutions. The Photographers’ Gallery puts the focus on colour this autumn, for example, with classic images by William Eggleston and colour portraits by Sanlé Sory, some of which are previously unseen. The National Portrait Gallery also embraces a rush of colour with an exhibition by Tim Walker, Fairyland , exploring queer identity, love and community. Tate Britain’s The 90s: Art and Fashion has just opened; the reviews have been mixed, it’s fair to say, but it features celebrated photographic projects by Juergen Teller, Eileen Perrier, and Nigel Shafran. Over at Tate Modern, Light and Magic: The Birth of Art Photography is a new show on Pictorialism which emphasises its international spread; a long-awaited exhibition, it looks set to revitalise interest in this long over-looked genre.

Graces Mews is presenting What Rose from the Cut , a new evolution of the hit feminist collage exhibition The Rose , put together by artist Justine Kurland, curator and collector Sarah Miller Meigs, the venue, plus Fiona Rogers, Parasol Foundation Curator of Women in Photography at the V&A and author of the recent book, Cut Out: A Feminist History of Photo Collage . Delving back into history with artists such as Claude Cahun, and right up to the present day with Keisha Scarville, it’s presenting an exciting take on an always-edgy form. Collage also features at Hauser and Wirth in a new presentation of Lorna Simpson’s work, which also features her paintings and sculpture; the exhibition is a double-hander and also features Cindy Sherman, including works from her new series Fabric Matrons.

Over at Phillida Reid, there’s a solo presentation by Joanna Piotrowska; Wyrwa is an installation of new works including images of the town in which the artist grew up, mounted in bespoke aluminium and hand-blown glass frameworks. The show also includes childhood drawings, folded and overturns, and close-cropped fragments from her father’s negatives, shown behind tinted-glass. Katherine Hubbard’s The Great Room at Studio Voltaire delves into the artist’s experience of caring for her mother, the medium of photography, and a very interesting-looking architectural installation; Phaidon is also celebrating work by women, launching a new book Great Women Photographers , which is edited by Charlotte Flint and includes image-makers such as Letizia Battaglia, Myriam Boulos and Rinko Kawauchi. The book is accompanied by an exhibition, hosted at Dorchester Collection’s 45 Park Lane.

Large Glass is giving Italian photographer Mario Cresci a second show, People I Care About , documenting people in the Southern Italian town Tricarico, between 1966 and 1967; also dating back to the 1960s is an exhibition by Daido Moriyama at Hamilton’s Gallery, picking out Japan’s abrupt shift into hypercapitalism, and Andy Warhol’s influence on the photographer’s work. Over at No.9 Cork Street, Frieze’s permanent gallery space in Mayfair, To Seek, To Find celebrates photographic commissions by the Mr & Mrs Smith hotel group, including classic commissions by Tina Barney and Martin Parr, and brand-new work by Kalpesh Lathigra.

And of course there’s much else to see beyond photography alone. Radical Living in the UK at William Morris Gallery is an interesting – even inspiring – survey show into alternative communities, dating back over the last 200 years but including Dial House, the self-sustaining anarcho-pacifist open house founded in 1967 by Penny Rimbaud and Gee Vaucher of punk band Crass. Es Devlin: Other Worlds at the Design Museum is a retrospective of the innovative artist and designer’s work with space, which has included installations, set design and kinetic sculptures. Cady Noland at Gagosian’s Davies Street gallery is the artist’s first UK exhibition in over 30 years; featuring new work conceived for the space, it explores the material and symbolic architecture of American identity, power structures, celebrity and racism. This Is Still Not a Pipe: The Afterlife of Magritte at Gagosian Gallery Grosvenor Hill is a reappraisal of the Surrealist painter which pairs his work with contemporary artists’, and emphasises his continuing relevance in our ever more image-saturated lives.

Frieze London and Frieze Masters are open from 14-18 October in Regent’s Park www.frieze.com/fairs/frieze-london
